The second factor is the importance of grassroots structures. Ukrainians have come to recognize the role of local communities, civic activists, and decentralized structures—especially military units—in building national identity. Popular units and leaders within them such as the Azov Brigade (Denys Prokopenko), the 3rd Assault Brigade (Andriy Biletsky), and the Khartiia Brigade (Oleh Kozhemyako) may become umbrella organizations for political movements. (Although its early roots were in far-right ideologies, Azov has the reputation of one of the most capable fighting units and one that cares about the lives of ordinary soldiers. It attracts volunteers from different age groups and gender, ethnic, and language backgrounds. Its commanders rarely take sides in political clashes.)
In sum, individuals who demonstrated leadership during the war and achieved military, technological, administrative, diplomatic, or humanitarian success will find themselves at the forefront of political competition after the war. The most successful postwar political forces will have strong national leaders with solid wartime credentials while relying on horizontal structures that emerged during the war, including volunteer networks, veterans groups, and informal associations of local community leaders.
In Search of a Unifying Figure
Amid public concerns over corruption and lingering questions about his wartime decisions, Zelensky's window of opportunity to be a national unifying figure has probably closed. But his political networks will give him a considerable opportunity to retain influence if he leaves office. Prior to his arrest in May 2026, Yermak—until then his closest aide—had launched a project to forge a coalition of military commanders, veterans, and volunteers with the goal of creating a new political force that could contest postwar elections under Zelensky's leadership. Since Yermak's arrest, Zelensky has continued this project on his own.
Zelensky has paid more attention to his standing and reputation among the military since he sacked Yermak in November 2025. Since the beginning of this year, he has participated in eight meetings with service members from various branches of the Armed Forces, suggesting that he is investing time and effort to rebuild support among veterans as a way to maintain political influence, whether he decides to run for another term or not.
On the other hand, former commander-in-chief Zaluzhny, now the ambassador to the United Kingdom, has emerged in the public consciousness as a strong contender for the presidency even though he has not yet declared his ambitions to run for office. He is a unique figure and is trusted both by moderates, who laud him for leading and modernizing the Armed Forces, and by radicals, who believe he is too strong to be subdued or corrupted by shadowy politics. At the same time, Zaluzhny is a political novice, and his knowledge of English and understanding of the economy, in particular, are significant shortcomings. He will have to prove to Ukrainians that he has the qualities to lead the country on the international stage through a turbulent postwar future.
Someone else may still yet emerge as a unifying figure. Ukraine needs its next leader not only to focus on healing a wounded nation, defending against Russian threats, and modernizing the economy, but also to unite political forces: If the first postwar president is accepted by moderates but not trusted by radicals, there is a high risk of dangerous civil division that will undermine medium- to long-term stability.
The Tough Task Ahead
On many occasions throughout its contemporary history, Ukraine has witnessed the emergence of new faces and new political forces. However, few of them survived the test of parliamentary democracy, especially when it came to coalition-building. Many leaders focused on their personal ambitions and created weak party structures that rose and fell in parallel with their own fate. Stronger political actors have tended to concentrate, if not monopolize, power in their hands at the expense of junior partners, and in some cases they went so far as to prosecute the opposition. Moreover, external influence, especially from Russia, has repeatedly turned heated domestic political competition into an existential fight. These factors remain and will frame postwar politics. Even if the terms of a ceasefire or peace settlement are satisfactory to most Ukrainians, the country's democracy will face its fair share of challenges.
Considering how bitter internal feuds undermined Ukrainian statehood in the past, Ukraine's key power brokers—including Zelensky, Zaluzhny, Budanov, Biletsky, and Prokopenko—should reach an agreement so that free and fair elections can be held across the country and then negotiate some form of power-sharing. Since all of them have armed men and women behind them, maintaining calm and ensuring that the next electoral cycle can proceed without voter intimidation will be critical. Ukraine has already seen in 1918–1921 a period of otamanshchyna, when anarchy and bitter power struggles between rebel warlords contributed to Ukraine being subjugated by Russia under Bolshevik rule. This time, Ukrainians must find a way to avoid bringing violence into the political process. It is vital that postwar election results be accepted and that power be peacefully transferred to the winners.
Ukraine's postwar leaders will have to decide how to reconcile national priorities—especially spending on defense and social welfare—with the demands of major donors like the International Monetary Fund and the EU, including those regarding democratic rights and the rule of law. They will also need to adapt domestic policies to the permanent threat from Russia without returning to martial law and without concentrating power under the executive.
So long as Ukraine is not a member of NATO or the EU, its leaders will have to build an agile and innovative national security architecture based on defense alliances and arrangements with other democracies, not only in Europe but also in the Middle East (Israel) and the Asia-Pacific (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and the Philippines). Postwar Ukraine might also embark on trying to reshape its neighborhood. Ukrainians will have a hard time feeling secure with neighboring Belarus under the puppet regime of Aleksander Lukashenko and with Moldova's Transnistria region still a Russian-controlled enclave. Once the war ends, or even pauses, Ukraine's leaders are likely to address these threats, ideally in collaboration with the West but potentially unilaterally. They will need a more expansive and sophisticated view of engaging with countries in Africa, Latin America, and elsewhere. Its new leaders will need to maintain an equal focus on national defense and on securing the economic resources and trade relationships necessary to mitigate domestic demographic decline and fuel reconstruction.
These challenges will require the emerging crop of leaders to display a high degree of statesmanship. They must understand that personality-driven politics, polarization, legislative gridlock, and failure to respect the rule of law were profound mistakes that almost cost Ukraine its independence and statehood. If the country is to win the peace, it will need leaders who can break from the past once and for all.
Petro Burkovskyi, executive director of the Ilko Kucheriv Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
Olexiy Haran, is a professor at the Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

articles.title: South Korea president stresses US alliance as many baffled by Trump order to cut exercises
articles.body:
South Korea president stresses US alliance as many baffled by Trump order to cut exercises
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — South Korea’s president said Tuesday a solid alliance with the U.S. strengthens the foundation of national security, as many South Koreans were baffled and concerned about U.S. President Donald Trump’s abrupt order to “substantially reduce” joint military exercises.
Trump made the surprise announcement in a social media post just before U.S. and South Korean soldiers began Monday’s annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which are largely designed to sharpen readiness against North Korean threats.
Trump cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran.
Trump’s move was apparently taken without consultations with South Korea and meant to reach out to Kim, deepening concerns about the reliability of the U.S.-South Korean alliance forged in the turmoil of the 1950-53 Korean War.
Confidence in the U.S. has already eroded among many South Koreans because of Trump’s tariff war and last year’s immigration raid in the U.S. state of Georgia that led to the detainment of hundreds of South Korean workers.
Trump’s announcement “reveals the stark reality of a faltering Korea-U.S. alliance, fueling public anxiety,” South Korea’s Hankook Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial Tuesday. “It’s absurd that the U.S. appears to treat North Korea more respectfully than its ally South Korea.”
South Korean leader calls for solid US alliance
In a regular Cabinet meeting, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung stressed the importance of a firm military alliance with the U.S., saying that “national security will be further strengthened when the alliance is solid.”
“When we build up our strengths, our value and importance as an ally will further grow,” said Lee, a liberal who has called for a stronger, self-reliant defense posture.
It was unclear which parts of the 11-day South Korea-U.S. exercises were being downsized. The South Korean and U.S. militaries earlier said their drills this year would be similar in scale to previous years and incorporate lessons from recent conflicts such as North Korea’s battlefield experiences in the Russia-Ukraine front. They also said the drills are defensive in nature.
North Korea’s Foreign Ministry accused South Korea and the U.S. of plotting more provocative drills this year and vowed to respond with “a new level of a deterrent.”
Prospects unclear for reengagement between Trump and Kim
Kim has shunned any talks with the U.S. and South Korea since his earlier high-profile diplomacy with Trump fell apart in 2019.
Experts say Kim won’t likely embrace Trump’s overture and return to talks anytime soon unless he is promised bigger U.S. concessions. Kim has boosted his military and diplomatic credentials in recent years by enlarging his nuclear arsenal and aligning with Russia over its war against Ukraine.
Lee’s presidential office on Monday expressed hopes that a “friendly relationship” between Trump and Kim would lead to “meaningful dialogue” between their countries to promote peace on the Korean Peninsula. That invited a backlash from conservatives, who criticized Lee’s government for allegedly prioritizing resumption of Kim-Trump diplomacy over security concerns.
“South Korea’s security bulwark is being shaken to its very foundations,” Park Chung-kwon, a spokesperson for the main conservative opposition People Power Party, said in a statement.
A weakening of the U.S. defense commitment could shake South Korea’s national security as it has no nuclear weapons and is under the so-called U.S. “nuclear umbrella” protection, which guarantees a devastating American response in the event of an attack on its ally by nuclear-armed North Korea. The U.S. has about 28,500 troops in South Korea.
Doubts about US alliance grow in South Korea
In his social media post, Trump said the military exercises with South Korea are not only costly but “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, which he said “has been unthreatening and respectful” during his time in the White House. Trump said he asked Lee if South Korea would join the U.S. in the “denuclearization” of Iran, “and they said, ‘No thanks!’”
Lee’s office said South Korea and the U.S. are closely discussing practical and military contributions that South Korea can make to help restore freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Trump thinks of an alliance as an investment that should pay regular dividends, or a rainy-day fund he can withdraw from when another project isn’t going well,” said Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.
“South Korean leaders understand that relations with the Trump administration will be a constant renegotiation linking economic and security issues. Seoul is thus cautiously responding to recent developments within that framework,” Easley said.
A recent survey jointly conducted by South Korea’s JoongAng Ilbo newspaper and the East Asia Institute, a Seoul-based research group, showed 46.4% of respondents in South Korea viewed the U.S. as “not a trustworthy partner” while 45.4% called it “trustworthy.”
It was the first time that more Koreans said they could not trust the U.S. than said they could since the East Asia Institute began asking the question in 2017, JoongAng Ilbo reported.

articles.title: North Korea steps up hacking with AI and deepfakes
articles.body:
- North Korea-linked groups carried out 99 state-sponsored cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, with South Korea targeted 19 times, the most of any country.
- Combined attacks from North Korea, China and Russia totaled 158 incidents, up 7.5 percent from the prior six months, according to S2W.
North Korea-linked hacking groups launched 99 state-sponsored cyberattacks in the first half of 2026, with South Korea absorbing 19 of them, the most of any country, the Korea Times reported, citing a new threat intelligence report from cybersecurity firm S2W.
The figure makes North Korea the most active state-backed threat actor globally over the period, ahead of China’s 33 incidents and Russia’s 26. Combined attacks from all three countries totaled 158 between January and June, up 7.5 percent from 147 in the second half of last year. Most of that growth came in the first quarter, driven by intensified activity from North Korean and Russian groups.
North Korea’s attack volume rose 13.8 percent compared with the previous six months, according to the S2W report. The United States was the second most targeted country by North Korean actors, with eight recorded attacks.
Pyongyang-linked groups concentrated on the cryptocurrency, IT and software development sectors, using fake job postings, code repository infiltration, generative AI and deepfakes to gain access. South Korean cybersecurity firm AhnLab has separately tracked North Korean-linked spear phishing campaigns against South Korean targets this year using malicious LNK and CHM file attachments to deploy backdoors and infostealers.
Russian-linked attacks rose 30 percent to 26 incidents, with 10 aimed at Ukraine. Russian groups also expanded into Eastern Europe, striking Poland and Romania twice each, targeting European government and military organizations alongside their Ukraine-focused activity. The S2W report found Russian operations increasingly combined intelligence gathering with destructive attacks meant to disrupt or destroy systems.
China-linked attacks fell 17.5 percent, from 40 to 33 incidents, with Chinese groups sustaining long-term espionage operations against the telecommunications sector while expanding into Southeast Asia and the Middle East. S2W’s analysis found Chinese operators relied on legitimate cloud APIs, VPNs and network tunneling tools alongside malware to maintain extended access to compromised networks.
Across all three countries, S2W identified 15 unique exploited vulnerabilities used in 19 separate incidents during the first half. North Korean groups relied primarily on social engineering and tricking users into executing malicious files, while Chinese groups exploited vulnerabilities in public-facing servers and network edge devices. Russian groups favored document-based malware along with webmail and network device vulnerabilities. Phishing, exploitation of public server vulnerabilities and abuse of proxy and cloud services were common across all three.
The report projected that infiltration of software development ecosystems, long-term access to telecommunications and infrastructure networks, and destructive operations tied to geopolitical conflicts will continue into the second half of the year. S2W also flagged Iran-linked groups as a risk to South Korean manufacturing, aviation and energy companies through Middle East-based supply chain attacks, saying the threat warrants close monitoring.
A cybersecurity expert cited in the report said organizations need to move beyond fragmented defenses focused solely on email and malware blocking toward integrated security frameworks covering development environments, supply chains, internet-facing assets, cloud systems and AI environments. The expert also called for stronger intrusion detection, immediate rotation of account credentials, and the buildup of immutable backup and recovery systems.

articles.title: The US-Iran MoU is dead. What killed it and what happens now?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The US-Iran MoU is dead. What killed it and what happens now?
The memorandum of understanding aimed at ending the war between Iran and the US expired on Monday, increasing the risk of a slide back towards open conflict and heightening uncertainty over a diplomatic settlement.
As the deadline edged closer, there was little sign of political will in either Washington or Tehran to extend the 60-day deal or return to the negotiating table.
Instead, the two sides have continued to trade threats, with US President Donald Trump threatening last week to declare the Strait of Hormuz an American territory and Iranian officials signalling readiness to return to war.
Here's what you need to know about the deal and why it failed.
What was agreed?
The interim deal was signed on 17 June by Trump and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and came following weeks of high-stakes diplomacy led by Pakistan and Qatar. It kick-started a two-month period during which the two sides committed to the ambitious goal of agreeing to a comprehensive peace agreement settling the intractable dispute over Tehran's nuclear programme.
Kicking the nuclear issue to future negotiations, the MoU was a stop-gap measure that nonetheless sought to address the most immediate crises by imposing a region-wide ceasefire and re-opening the Strait of Hormuz.
Under the deal, both sides agreed to immediately and permanently end military operations across all fronts, including in Lebanon, and to refrain from threats or the use of force.
To resolve the crisis in the strait, the US agreed to lift its blockade on Iranian ports within 30 days in return for Iran lifting restrictions on traffic and demining the area. Tehran said it would waive all fees for 60 days while the final deal was being negotiated. Crucially, it separated the strait's future status from the US-Iran negotiations, empowering Tehran to work with Oman to decide how it would be administered after the war.
Meanwhile, the US agreed to terminate all sanctions on Iran, issue waivers for its oil exports, and unlock some of its frozen assets. It also committed to develop a plan that would see at least $300 billion invested in Iran's reconstruction and economic development.
Iran reiterated its commitment not to seek nuclear weapons and agreed to freeze all nuclear activity while negotiations for a final deal continued.
Why has it failed?
Iran and the US showed goodwill in the days after the agreement, travelling to Switzerland on 21 June for what was the highest-level meeting between Iranian and American officials in decades. The following day, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Iran's oil exports for two months.
But things began to unravel in the subsequent weeks, with the countries trading accusations of breaching the accord.
On 26 June, Trump accused Iran of a "foolish violation" after a cargo ship was attacked in the Strait. Two days later, Tehran said Washington had broken the agreement following renewed US strikes. At the heart of the disagreement was the strait, which US officials continued to insist should be returned to its pre-war status quo. Iranian officials meanwhile bristled as Trump resumed his incendiary rhetoric, which they said violated the deal.
Officials from both countries soon declared the death of the MoU, and by the middle of July the ceasefire had all but collapsed. For two weeks, the US bombarded southern Iran while Tehran resumed heavy strikes across the Gulf.
Since a fragile peace was restored at the end of the month, there have been few signs that the warring countries are prepared to return to the negotiating table. Instead, both countries have returned to sabre-rattling and contesting control of the strait. Meanwhile, there has been no movement on US sanctions or Iran's frozen assets, while the American military has reimposed its blockade.
"The expiration of the MoU is, in one sense, the formal recognition of a reality that had already emerged," Neil Quilliam, Middle East foreign policy specialist at Chatham House, told The New Arab.
Both countries had already called the deal into question and accused one another of breaking its terms. "In that respect, the end of the MoU confirms the death of a framework that was already struggling to survive," he said.
What happens now?
The wider significance of its expiry lies in what happens next.
"If no alternative framework emerges, both sides will have greater freedom to pursue coercive measures, including military pressure, without the constraints, however weak, imposed by the agreement," Quilliam said. "This increases uncertainty and the risk of miscalculation."
Rather than threatening a military attack, Trump officials have instead signalled a return to economic pressure, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent vowing to impose measures that "have never been seen in the history of economic isolation".
The American military's ability to continue defending against Iranian attacks has been called into question in recent weeks following reports of a severe depletion of missile interceptors. It has also been said to have used "virtually all" of its precision long-range missiles.
Iran meanwhile has vowed to resume the war if the US does not agree to its demands. An Iranian official threatened on Monday to go "fully offensive" and escalate in the Gulf in a bid to break the US blockade.
Quilliam said the most likely outcome is a prolonged period of on-off confrontation. Neither side will likely risk a major regional war, but the profound lack of trust will continue to impede meaningful negotiations.
"Barring a major provocation, both Washington and Tehran appear more likely to manage tensions than seek a direct military showdown," he said.
"The danger is that prolonged instability creates repeated opportunities for miscalculation, making the conflict harder to contain over time."

articles.title: Russia warns UK of ‘consequences’ over reports Ukraine using British drones in attacks
articles.body:
Moscow has threatened the UK with “consequences” after reports that British drones have been used to strike targets on Russia’s mainland for the first time.
Ukraine used drones made by two UK companies as part of a so-called deep-strike campaign, the Sunday Times reported.
Kyiv has stepped up its attacks on Russia this year, with long-range missiles and swarms of drones increasingly targeting military industries and energy facilities.
It has also targeted giant depots for Wildberries, Russia’s largest online retailer, burning billions of pounds’ worth of merchandise and bringing the war home to the Russian public more than four years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia’s embassy to the UK said in a statement on Monday that the reports “confirm that London is deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis” and accused Britain of “seeking to contain Russia and inflict maximum damage on it by proxy”.
“London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer,” it said. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kyiv’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”
A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “Britain stands shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and we are committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against Putin’s illegal invasion.
“Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies.”
Ukraine’s strategy of long-range drone strikes is thought to be intended to cut Moscow’s revenue for the war and make Russian citizens feel the impact of the invasion.
It launched three times as many such strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from Acled, an independent conflict monitor.
Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced Moscow to stretch air defences over a larger area. Russia’s defence ministry said on Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions as well as the Black Sea, the Azov Sea and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
Officials said on Monday that Ukrainian long-range attacks on Russia killed seven people overnight, while five civilians died in Ukraine after strikes by Moscow’s forces.
Russian missile attacks on Tuesday killed 10 people and injured a eight in a village in Ukraine’s north-eastern Kharkiv oblast, the regional governor said.
The strike on the village of Pechenihy damaged 10 private buildings, a cafe, a post office, a shop and at least seven cars, Oleh Syniehubov said on Telegram.
A rapid development of largely homegrown technologies, including the Flamingo cruise missile and the FP-1 long-range fixed-wing drone from Fire Point, have allowed Ukraine to bomb warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities up to 1,500 miles (2,400km) from its border.
Ukraine can now almost match the deep-strike capability that Russia has had since the beginning of the war using large drones and cruise missiles, though it does not possess the high-speed ballistic missiles that Moscow frequently uses.
At the same time, both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion, leading to a rise in civilian casualties and worries that the impact of the conflict beyond the immediate frontlines will only increase into the winter.

articles.title: Russia tests new submarine designed for ultra long-range nuclear torpedo
articles.body:
- The Russian Navy's Khabarovsk submarine began factory sea trials on August 17, its first time underway since construction started in 2014.
- The Project 09851 submarine is designed to carry six Poseidon nuclear-powered underwater drones and is expected to join the Pacific Fleet.
Russia’s Northern Machine-Building Enterprise sent the nuclear-powered submarine Khabarovsk to sea for factory trials on August 17, the vessel’s first time underway since construction began in 2014, according to Russian defense-monitoring channels.
The submarine, built under Project 09851 at the Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk, is designed to carry the Poseidon (NATO name: KANYON) nuclear-powered underwater drone system. Russia’s Rubin Central Design Bureau for Marine Engineering designed the vessel under a contract signed with the Russian Ministry of Defense on June 19, 2012. Construction formally began July 27, 2014.
Khabarovsk was floated out of its construction hall on November 1, 2025, ahead of Monday’s sea trials. The submarine’s contract had originally called for delivery to the Russian Navy in 2020, though reports have not disclosed the reason for the six-year delay.
The vessel is believed to carry six 2P39 launch tubes for the 2M39 Poseidon underwater vehicles. Russian media have described each Poseidon as roughly 66 feet (20 meters) long, about six feet (1.8 meters) in diameter and weighing around 110 tons. Analysts have assessed its range at approximately 6,200 miles (10,000 kilometers), though claims of a 100-knot top speed have not been independently confirmed.
President Vladimir Putin said Russia conducted its first test involving an activated nuclear power unit on the Poseidon on October 28, 2025, launching the weapon from a submarine.
“For the first time, we managed not only to launch it with a launch engine from a carrier submarine, but also to launch the nuclear power unit on which this device passed a certain amount of time,” Putin said.
“There is nothing like this,” Putin said of the weapon, one of six strategic systems he first revealed publicly in 2018.
That October test has not been independently verified. Some Western observers noted the presence of six unidentified vessels off Novaya Zemlya in the Kara Sea on the day Putin said the test occurred, though no confirming movement of Russian support ships or NATO surveillance assets was widely reported at the time.
Photographs of Khabarovsk’s float-out show a stern section, propulsion system and rudders nearly identical to those on Russia’s modified Borei-A class ballistic missile submarines, according to Russian defense channels.
Khabarovsk will join Russia’s Pacific Fleet once trials conclude. Russia previously delivered its first Poseidon carrier, the submarine Belgorod, to the Navy on July 8, 2022. Belgorod, built under Project 09852, was converted from an unfinished Project 949A cruise missile submarine and carries four 2P39 launch tubes rather than six. Russia has said it plans to field a total of five Poseidon-armed submarines.
Rubin’s design bureau reported plans in 2016 to begin design work on a follow-on vessel, Project 09853, believed to be a modified or serial version of the Khabarovsk design. No public reporting has confirmed that construction of a Project 09853 submarine has begun.
Russia is building a dedicated submarine base for the Project 09851 and 09852 vessels, along with their Project 20183 support ship, at Kraсheninnikov Bay on the Kamchatka Peninsula.

articles.title: Iran requires Qatar clarifying fate of four Iranian pilots
articles.body:
Speaking at his weekly press briefing on Monday, Iran's Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei emphasized that Tehran does not formulate its policies under pressure or artificial deadlines and that the United States has violated the MoU from the outset.
There was no provision in the text of the memorandum of understanding (MoU) establishing a 60-day deadline, explaining that the document only envisaged negotiations on the nuclear issue within 60 days, he stated.
“We did not start any negotiations at all, and the US violated the understanding from the very beginning; therefore, the 60-day issue is not relevant,” he said.
Baghaei emphasized that Iran would make decisions based on its national interests and assessments rather than being compelled by a deadline.
“Iran is not a party that adjusts its policies under pressure and deadlines,” he underlined.
The spokesperson also said Iran’s Armed Forces are closely monitoring developments, stressing that “Our powerful Armed Forces are keeping a watchful eye on any movement.” He added that strengthening relations with regional countries is part of Iran’s ongoing activities.
Addressing US claims that Washington had changed its priorities regarding Iran, Baghaei said the claims demonstrates continued confusion and confirmed that the war of aggression against Iran had no basis other than serving the ambitions of “a regime in our region.”
He said the US had initially cited the need to confront an imminent threat from Iran as the reason for launching the war, but the Pentagon itself has rejected the claim and said there had been no such threat.
“They have trapped themselves in a quagmire and, in order to justify their failures, they are forced to change their objectives,” Baghaei said.
He added that Washington’s concern has now shifted to the Strait of Hormuz, which he said had been open before the aggression.
“Under these circumstances, the best thing for the US is to extricate itself as soon as possible before becoming more deeply involved,” Baghaei said, adding that acknowledging a mistake could pave the way for a correct decision, although he expressed doubt that US officials possessed “such courage.”
In response to a question on the fate of four Iranian pilots who went missing after Iran's March 2 strike on a US military base in Qatar and were captured alive in this country, Baghaei underlined that Tehran has been using diplomatic contacts and all available channels to determine the fate of four Iranian pilots who went missing during a defensive operation against a US military target in Qatar.
Tehran has been using diplomatic contacts and all available channels to determine the fate of four Iranian pilots who went missing during a defensive operation against a US military target in Qatar, the spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry stated.
He said Iran maintains regular contacts with Qatar and has conveyed its concerns and considerations to the Qatari side regarding the missing pilots.
The spokesperson stressed that Tehran is seriously demanding clarification of the fate of the Iranian Air Force personnel who had been dispatched on a defensive mission “to target the source of the US aggression.”
“We have been pursuing the issue since the very day we became aware of it,” Baghaei said, adding that he was present with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi when the latter was informed about the matter on the evening of the first days of the US-Israeli war of aggression, after which the pilots’ fate was immediately placed on the agenda.
Baghaei said Iran sent its first correspondence to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) on February 15, while the Iranian Embassy in Doha also began following up on the matter from those early days.
“As long as their status has not been clarified, the assumption is that they have been captured, and we are using all capacities to determine the status of the pilots,” he said.
He reiterated that the fate of the four pilots had been pursued from the earliest days, emphasizing that “they were on a defensive operation.”
Iran has recently made public for the first time its assessment that three of the pilots who went missing after a March 2 operation against the US-operated Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar were captured alive by Qatari forces.
Brigadier General Mohammad Bagherzadeh, commander of the Missing in Action Search Committee of Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff, raised the issue in a letter to ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric Egger on August 15, expressing grave concern over their fate and urging the organization to investigate their condition and facilitate their release.
According to Bagherzadeh, two Iranian Air Force Su-24s carried out the mission but were hit by enemy air defenses while returning, forcing their crews to eject. One of the four pilots, Brigadier General Majid Kazemi, was martyred, with DNA testing later confirming his death and his remains returned to Iran. Baqerzadeh identified the three other pilots as Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian and Omran Behraveshian, saying they had been captured alive by Qatari forces.
The Iranian military official said Tehran had been unable, despite diplomatic follow-ups, to meet or interview the three pilots or establish contact between them and their families. He cited provisions of the Third Geneva Convention concerning prisoners of war and called on the ICRC to urgently establish contact with the pilots, report on their health and help secure their “swift release.”
The disclosure followed months of uncertainty over the pilots’ whereabouts. Iranian officials have repeatedly urged Qatar to clarify their status and act in accordance with international humanitarian law, while Qatari authorities have said they had no information about the missing airmen. The March 2 operation came amid Iran’s broader military response to US and Israeli attacks that began on February 28.

Russian Banderol Missile Reportedly Crosses Into Moldova and Explodes Near Tălmaza
A Russian "Banderol" loitering munition crossed from Odesa region into Moldova on August 17, Ukraine's Air Force reported, before an unidentified aircraft crashed near the village of Tălmaza in the country's Ștefan Vodă district.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In posts published on Telegram at 5:30 and 5:40 p.m., the Ukrainian Air Force first tracked the munition moving northwest past Odesa, then announced it had crossed the state border toward Moldova.
Moldovan police noted that officers were alerted to an explosion outside Tălmaza that evening, roughly three kilometers from the village, after an aircraft they characterized only as "unidentified" struck the ground, Moldova1 added.
Emergency crews extinguished the fire and secured the area, and no casualties were recorded, the police confirmed.
Specialists from the technical-explosive section were sent to examine the wreckage and establish the object's origin. Authorities urged residents to avoid the site and not to touch any debris, citing the risk from possible explosive components.
Moldovan police did not link the wreckage to the loitering munition tracked by Ukraine's Air Force, and no official assessment has established that the two are the same object. The characterization of the crashed aircraft remained open pending the technical-explosive examination.
Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR) has published technical details of Russia’s S8000 “Banderol” cruise missile through its War & Sanctions platform, including an interactive 3D model showing the weapon’s airframe and folding-wing mechanism.
The S8000 Banderol is a compact, low-cost cruise missile built by the Russian manufacturer Kronshtadt and typically air-launched from Orion reconnaissance drones or Mi-8 helicopters. It carries a high-explosive fragmentation warhead with roughly 50 kilograms of explosive filler and a theoretical range of up to 500 kilometers, though Ukrainian forces have documented strikes only at distances up to 300 kilometers.
Such incursions have become a recurring hazard along Moldova's frontier, forcing the authorities to close portions of the country's airspace as Russian strike packages aimed at Ukraine drift across the border.
In May, a Russian drone crossed from Ukraine's Vinnytsia region toward the northern village of Sauca, prompting a temporary closure of parts of Moldovan airspace during a mass bombardment of its neighbor.

A Russian missile strike on the village of Pechenyhy in the Kharkiv region killed 10 people and injured 17 on Tuesday, Aug. 18, according to local authorities.
Kharkiv Regional Military Administration (OVA) Head Oleh Syniehubov said the injured were receiving medical treatment.

The strike damaged 10 private homes, as well as a cafe, post office and shop. At least seven cars were also damaged.
Emergency crews were working at the scene to clear the consequences of the attack.
Later, Syniehubov clarified that the number of people injured in the attack had risen from 8 to 17.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has also reacted to the strike, writing on social media:
“This morning, the Russians brutally struck a crowded intersection in Pechenyhy, Kharkiv region, where the post office and shops are located, surrounded by residential buildings.”
He expressed his condolences to the families and friends of those killed. According to Zelensky, rescuers have already extinguished the fire, while emergency and other services continue to work at the scene. The circumstances of the attack are being investigated.
“We will definitely respond to this Russian strike. And it is no less important that partners also complement our fair kinetic responses with their steps in putting pressure on Russia and supporting Ukraine,” the president added.
Russian drones hit Kyiv region and Zaporizhzhia
Russian drones also attacked Kyiv region early Tuesday, damaging civilian infrastructure in the Brovary district.

articles.title: The 60-day deadline for an Iran peace deal is expiring. Here’s where things stand
articles.body:
The 60-day deadline for an Iran peace deal is expiring. Here’s where things stand
The deal that U.S. President Donald Trump signed at Versailles in June set an ambitious 60-day deadline for ending the war with Iran and reaching an accord on its nuclear program.
The deadline was Monday, and the two sides are further apart than they were then.
Talks, such as they are, have focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting a U.S. blockade on Iran, both of which were supposed to have happened under the interim deal. There has been no sign of any compromise on the strait, or that detailed nuclear talks have even begun.
The U.S., meanwhile, has no good options for getting out of the war it started alongside Israel.
Acceding to Iran’s latest demands would mean giving it control over a critical international waterway that carried a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas before the war — and would be tantamount to admitting defeat. Escalating the deeply unpopular war would further draw down U.S. supplies of advanced missile interceptors, jolt the world economy, and drive up gas prices ahead of U.S. congressional elections.
So both sides have dug in, hoping the other will blink first. So far, neither has.
The interim deal collapsed weeks later
The June deal, known as the Memorandum of Understanding, called for a halt to all military operations and set a 60-day deadline for an agreement to permanently end the war and resolve the longstanding dispute over Iran’s nuclear activities.
It called for the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened but gave Iran a vaguely defined role in facilitating traffic, leaving open the possibility it could charge fees after the 60-day deadline. Iran has seized on that clause to claim control over the waterway.
A week after the deal was signed, Iran began firing on vessels using a route along the coast of Oman, on the other side of the strait, that is overseen by the U.S. military and intended to bypass Tehran’s control.
The U.S. responded by striking Iran, which retaliated by attacking Arab countries hosting American forces, like Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain. The U.S. canceled waivers issued as part of the deal that had allowed Iran to sell its oil internationally and Trump restored a blockade of Iran’s ports.
Each side accused the other of violating the June agreement, of which almost nothing remains.
The fighting eventually died down. A related truce in Lebanon between Israel and the Iran-backed Hezbollah has mostly held, even as Israeli troops occupy large areas in the country’s south. Lebanon’s “territorial integrity and sovereignty” were to have been ensured under the June deal.
Iranian officials say they stopped negotiating with the U.S. in June, while acknowledging that messages have been relayed by intermediaries. Trump says the talks have continued, occasionally claiming progress after pulling back from threatening major strikes.
Pakistan, which played a key role in brokering the June agreement, noted last week that the deadline was Monday while expressing hope it would be extended.
“We are not closing the chapter,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Tahir Andrabi said. “Pakistan is making all-out efforts to bring the two parties to the negotiating table.”
Iran’s leaders think they can force Trump to give up the strait
Earlier this month, Iran issued a list of demands for reopening the strait, including the lifting of the American blockade, the withdrawal of U.S. forces from around Iran and the payment of reparations for damage inflicted in the war started by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28.
Even then, Iran has said it would control the strait — and potentially charge fees — through an agreement it is negotiating with Oman, and that the strait will not go back to being an open, toll-free waterway as it was before the war.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have meanwhile begun attacking Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, threatening another crucial trade route that had been used to relieve some of the pressure from the strait being closed.
Trump has rejected Iran’s demands — saying it’s Tehran that should pay war reparations and claiming the U.S. controls the strait. He appears to be banking on economic pressure — in the form of the blockade and longstanding sanctions — to bring Iran’s rulers to their knees.
Iran’s economy has been battered by the war and isolation, and inflation has soared. The crisis could stoke renewed anti-government protests, like those that were brutally crushed in January.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which rose immediately after the interim deal, is back to a small fraction of what it was before the war. Rising prices of fuel and other goods are expected to climb further the longer this continues with effects far beyond the Middle East.
The clock is still ticking for both sides.
___
Associated Press writer Munir Ahmed in Islamabad contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russia Builds 10 New Drone Bases Near NATO Borders, With Warsaw Potentially Within Range
articles.body:

Russia Builds 10 New Drone Bases Near NATO Borders, With Warsaw Potentially Within Range
Russia has established at least 10 new or upgraded drone facilities near its borders with Belarus and Ukraine, including launch sites that could eventually place NATO territory within range of Moscow’s most advanced long-range attack drones, The Telegraph reported on August 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The newspaper identified at least 59 newly constructed launch rails across western Russia using leaked documents and satellite imagery. The infrastructure includes former military bases and civilian airfields that have been converted for drone operations.
Some of the facilities are already supporting Russian strikes against Ukraine. Their location close to the Ukrainian border allows Russian forces to launch large-scale drone attacks while shortening the distance their aircraft need to travel before reaching Ukrainian airspace.
Analysts caution that Russia could potentially redirect the rapidly advancing drone technology toward Europe in a future conflict, with some of the newly established bases placing Warsaw within range of its most capable long-range UAVs.
Imagery analyzed by drone intelligence company DroneSec showed that around 20 of the newly installed launch rails are longer than the others, potentially indicating that they are intended for Russia’s newest long-range drones.
The investigation also found substantial storage capacity at some of the facilities. One site reportedly has enough space to accommodate more than 1,000 drones, while additional launch rails are being built at several locations.
The facilities are reportedly supplied by Russian drone and ammunition manufacturers, including companies operating in the Alabuga special economic zone, a major center of Russia’s drone production.
The buildup comes as European and US intelligence officials warn of the possibility of Russian provocations against NATO members. Potential scenarios include attacks on critical infrastructure in Poland, missile or drone strikes, and false-flag operations intended to implicate Ukraine.
A NATO official told The Telegraph that the alliance remains prepared to defend allied territory and is strengthening its capabilities to respond to threats, including those posed by drones.
“This launch site expansion shows how Russia has expanded its ability to launch greater numbers of drones while at the same time using technology to make the types of drones used more difficult to intercept,” said Mike Monnik, the chief executive and founder of DroneSec.
The development comes as US intelligence has cautioned European allies that Russia could be preparing “hybrid” operations in Europe, with Poland and the Baltic states considered potential targets.
The Central Intelligence Agency warned of possible attacks on critical infrastructure, including sabotage, as well as false-flag operations. However, intelligence officials said Moscow could also be deliberately creating the impression that such attacks are being planned as part of an effort to fuel fear and uncertainty in Europe.

articles.title: Ukrainian intelligence agency names 10 more individuals involved in militarisation of Ukrainian children under occupation
articles.body:
Ukrainian intelligence agency names 10 more individuals involved in militarisation of Ukrainian children under occupation
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has published data on 10 more individuals and two legal entities involved in the militarisation of Ukrainian children under Russian occupation.
Source: DIU
Details: Among them is the so-called deputy minister of education, science and youth of Crimea.
In May 2026, a competition called Zarnitsa 2.0 was held in temporarily occupied territories (TOT) by Russia, organised by the pro-Putin youth movement Movement of the First (Dvizheniye Pervykh).
During the event, children were taught to handle weapons and explosives and to operate drones. DIU says militarist propaganda was disseminated among the participants of the competition.
"The purpose of such activities is to destroy Ukrainian identity in children and prepare them to participate in the criminal war against their own country.
The aggressor state is carrying out the forcible ideological 'reprogramming' of Ukrainian children in the TOT and shaping a future pool of recruits for its army in pursuit of its aggressive neo-imperial policy," the intelligence agency explained.
Among those involved is Russian national Artur Orlov, who heads Movement of the First. The organisation participates in the mass abduction, illegal deportation and forced displacement of children and conducts "military-patriotic" education of young people and prepares them for service in the Russian military.
"Orlov is a veteran of the armed aggression against Ukraine and holds the title of 'Hero of Russia'. He regularly holds meetings with participants of Movement of the First who are taking part in the so-called Special Military Operation (SMO)," DIU said.
The list also includes Svetlana Bespalova, the so-called deputy minister of education, science and youth of the occupation administration in Crimea. The official facilitates the integration of the peninsula's educational institutions into the Russian system and participates in the implementation of Russian policy in the sphere of education, science and youth upbringing.
In October 2023, a ceremonial unveiling of a memorial wall to "SMO heroes" took place in Crimea. At the event, Bespalova stated that a unified system of "patriotic education" was being established in Crimea.
"Commenting in April 2026 on the results of a working meeting on the preparation of textbooks for the course 'History of Our Region', she stressed that their content should be based on so-called traditional Russian spiritual and moral values," the intelligence report states.
Regional leaders of Dvizheniye Pervykh also contribute to the militarisation of children: Aleksei Lavrentyev, Marina Tsvetinskaya, Riyal Asif Ogly Aliyev, Yekaterina Kozyr and Viktoria Kostromina.
Lavrentyev organised a local stage of the Zarnitsa 2.0 game in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast. During the competition, he stated that children needed to honour the traditions of Russia's military affairs.
Kostromina, together with Yunarmiya, participated in a flower-laying ceremony at the monument to Bohdan Khmelnytskyi. She said at the time that the younger generation should remember the history of "accession to the Russian Federation" following the Council of Pereiasliv.
The list was extended by Nikita Polyakov, chief of staff of the regional branch of Russia's Yunarmiya in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast.
Among the institutions facilitating militarisation is the youth centre Selet-AK Bars of the Ministry of Youth Affairs of the Republic of Tatarstan, which operates on the territory of Crimea.
Secondary school No. 5 in Simferopol and its so-called principal Dmitry Prividyon were also added to the list. According to DIU, the educational institution regularly holds events aimed at re-educating and militarising children from the temporarily occupied territories. The school's "head" himself visits combat positions of the Russian military and delivers humanitarian aid from pupils and staff to them.
Background:
- The Back to Ukraine initiative previously established that Ukrainian national Oleksandr Mustiace, who as a child found himself under occupation after 2022, joined the Russian military.
- Due to the absence of posts on his social media, it was assumed that the young man had been killed. However, his current page was later found. He stated that "Russia has always been in his heart".
- Activists subsequently established that Oleksandr's 15-year-old brother is a member of the militarised Yunarmiya movement and is under the guardianship of Anna Nazarova. The woman may be the head of the Social Protection Department of the Pervomaisky district of Rostov-on-Don.

articles.title: Iran working to finalize Hormuz agreement with Oman, and other news from the Middle East
articles.body:
Trump threatens Oman as it works with Iran on a Strait of Hormuz deal, and other Middle East news
U.S. President Donald Trump has again threatened Oman as Iran says it is working with the Gulf Arab country on a plan to manage shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Fully reopening the waterway has been a key U.S. demand.
Meanwhile, the 60-day negotiating period to find a peace deal between the United States and Iran was expiring, with no word of an extension and both sides seemingly as far apart as they were at the start.
Here’s a look at the latest developments Monday in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Iran says it is near finalizing a deal with Oman
Iran said it has reached an agreement with Oman over a plan for ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which runs between the two countries, and they are now working to finalize details for a joint statement.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told reporters in Tehran, Iran’s capital, that “an understanding has been reached regarding the map of the transit route.”
He did not elaborate, but details that have previously emerged suggest the deal would reopen the strait with ships entering through a route close to Iran and exiting through a route close to Oman. Ships would transit without paying fees or tolls during an interim period.
The U.S. has sought an acceptable deal on opening the strait before ending its blockade of Iranian ports.
Iran effectively closed the strait — through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s traded oil supplies passed before the war — after Israel and the U.S. attacked the country on Feb. 28.
Trump says US will bomb Oman if it gets in the way
Trump told Fox News reporter Trey Yingst that the U.S. would bomb Oman if it “gets in the way,” using an expletive for emphasis.
Fox News did not provide audio of the interview.
This is not the first time that Trump has threatened Oman. In May, he told reporters during a Cabinet meeting that “Oman will behave just like everybody else, or we will have to blow them up.”
Trump also said the expiration of the 60-day deadline on talks to end the war was irrelevant and said there was no timeline, Yingst said. Trump said the U.S. has a back channel for talks with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Yingst added.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres wants Iran and the U.S. to resume peace negotiations, saying there is no military solution to the conflict, according to U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric.
Dujarric said the U.N. chief also thinks the countries need to “lower the rhetoric that we’ve been hearing in recent days.”
Kushner meets with Netanyahu over Gaza road map
Mideast negotiator Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, met on Monday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the day after he had a rare, two-hour meeting with Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya in Egypt on disarmament of the Palestinian militant group.
Netanyahu last week rejected a 15-point, U.S.-backed road map to move the ceasefire deal forward in Gaza.
Hamas says it has agreed to the road map, which includes disarmament, and the group is urging mediators and the U.S.-created Board of Peace to “compel” Israel to sign on.
But Israel, which under the road map must gradually withdraw from Gaza, says Hamas must fully disarm before any Israeli withdrawal.
Israeli troops occupy about 60% of the strip, and Netanyahu has previously threatened to advance further.
Houthi rebels say they attacked boats in the Red Sea
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed that they attacked a ship and four military boats on Monday in the Red Sea off the Yemeni city of Mokha, near the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The rebels fired a number of ballistic missiles at the vessels, resulting in the capsizing and burning of the boats, Yahya Saree, a military spokesperson for the Houthis, said in a statement.
The rebels claimed that the vessels belonged to Saudi Arabia, without providing evidence. There was no immediate comment from Saudi Arabia, and The Associated Press could not independently verify the Houthi claim.
Saree also said the rebels launched a drone attack on government forces in the central province of Marib.
Drone attacks target Iraqi officials
Two officials in northern Iraq were targeted in drone attacks that the regional counterterrorism service said were launched from the border with Iran.
One was fired at the office of Masrour Barzani, prime minister of Iraq’s semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region, and the other targeted the home of a top regional intelligence official, the counterterrorism service said.
There were no casualties and no immediate claim of responsibility.
Since the beginning of the war in Iran, Tehran and Iranian-backed Iraqi militias have launched regular attacks on U.S. military and diplomatic facilities in Iraq, and on bases of exiled Iranian Kurdish dissident groups, but Monday’s direct attack on regional government buildings was unusual.
Barzani on X called the attack “a dangerous escalation and a direct threat to the security and stability” of the region.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi appeared to be trying to distance Iran from the attack. He said on social media that nothing justified the attack on Barzani and that “Kurdish friends should be vigilant against false-flag ploys to sow discord between neighbors.”
U.S. forces currently stationed in the Kurdish region of Iraq have begun withdrawing ahead of a Sept. 30 deadline agreed upon between Washington and Baghdad to end the U.S. military presence in Iraq.
___
This story was corrected earlier to show that the first name of the prime minister of Iraq’s semi-autonomous northern Kurdish region is Masrour Barzani, instead of Masoud Barzani.

articles.title: French Rafale intercepts Russian Tu-214 tied to FSB leadership
articles.body:
- French Rafale jets completed a four-month NATO Baltic Air Policing deployment logging 540 flight hours, 39 Alpha Scrambles and 69 Tango Scrambles.
- A French Rafale shot down a suspected Ukrainian drone over Latvia on June 8, and the pilots later received Latvian honors.
The French Air and Space Force released a summary of its four-month deployment to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission, including a photograph of a Rafale fighter intercepting a Russian Tupolev Tu-214 over the Baltic Sea.
The French service, known as the Armée de l’Air et de l’Espace, posted the recap on X, crediting the detachment with 540 flight hours, 39 Alpha Scrambles and 69 Tango Scrambles between April 1 and July 31. Alpha Scrambles are real-world alerts launched to identify unknown aircraft. Tango Scrambles are training intercepts.
Aviation journalist Piotr Butowski identified the intercepted aircraft in the photo as carrying an LSZ-100 laser self-defense system.
“A Tu-214, intercepted by the French over the Baltic Sea, has an LSZ-100 laser self-defence system (follow the arrow). If my notes are correct, this RA-64534 is the one the FSB leadership is using. The LSZ-100 and LSZ-200 systems are also on the Il-96-300s flown by Putin,” Butowski wrote.
Flight-tracking and aircraft registry records identify RA-64534 as a Tu-214PU variant operated by Russia’s Federal Security Service, the FSB. The Tu-214PU is a command and communications configuration of the airliner used to transport senior Russian officials.
France’s contribution ran under the 71st Baltic Air Policing mandate, its 12th participation in the mission since 2007, according to the French Ministry of Armed Forces. Four twin-seat Rafale B jets from Saint-Dizier Air Base flew the first two months, from April 1 to May 31. Four single-seat Rafale C jets from Mont-de-Marsan Air Base took over for the remainder, through July 31. Roughly 200 airmen rotated through the deployment at Šiauliai Air Base in Lithuania.
The detachment also covered air surveillance along Poland’s eastern border against unauthorized drone or missile incursions, the ministry said. Crews trained alongside Estonian and Lithuanian air forces on drone detection and interception, and most Rafale C training missions included at least one partner nation, principally Romania and Poland.
The deployment’s most significant event came on June 8, when a French Rafale C shot down a suspected Ukrainian attack drone over Latvia. Captain Josselin, who fired the shot, was on his first overseas operation and his first real-world Alpha Scramble. He and Lieutenant Colonel Romain later received Latvia’s Atzinības Goda Zīme honor from Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis for the intercept.
The French detachment operated on alternating alert postures, the ministry said, with “hot” weeks requiring a 15-minute launch capability and “cold” weeks allowing a three-hour response window.
The Baltic Air Policing mission has tracked a sharp rise in Russian military air activity along NATO’s eastern flank. NATO’s Allied Joint Force Command in Brunssum reported a 250 percent increase in scramble launches for enhanced Air Policing missions between July 2025 and July 2026, compared with the previous 12-month period.
France’s Rafales left Lithuania on August 1 and were relieved by four Eurofighter EF2000s from Italy’s Aeronautica Militare. The French Ministry of Armed Forces has not disclosed further detail on the specific circumstances of the Tu-214 intercept shown in the recap photo, including the date or the aircraft’s flight route.

articles.title: Iraq's parliament probes US-Saudi strikes on PMF HQ
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq's parliament investigates US-Saudi strikes on PMF headquarters
Iraqi sources said the circumstances surrounding the US-Saudi strikes on the headquarters of Iraqi factions, which took place at the end of last month, remain unclear after statements circulated claiming that senior Iraqi leaders had advanced information of the strikes.
This prompted the Iraqi parliament's Security and Defence Committee to seek an investigation into the circumstances and host senior leaders of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) and prominent security officials to establish the facts and determine the details.
This strikes have set of growing repercussions, as well as doubts and questions raised in recent days about the security precautionary measures taken before the PMF headquarters were targeted and whether there had been any particular failure.
The committee, headed by MP Khalid al-Obeidi, issued an official letter inviting senior security and military officials, including PMF chief Falih al-Fayyadh and Chief of Staff Abdul Aziz al-Muhammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
Those invited also include the director of the office of the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Abdul Amir al-Shammari; the army chief of staff, Abdul Amir Yarallah; and the senior Interior Ministry undersecretary, Hussein al-Awadi.
The letter stated that they would appear today at the committee's headquarters in the parliament building to determine why precautionary and security measures were not taken and why the headquarters was evacuated before the attack.
According to a member of the parliamentary committee, "The request to establish the facts and the attendance of the requested leaders came following accusations and statements that there had been advance information before the attack and that there had been a failure to perform the duty and evacuate the faction headquarters."
The member told The New Arab, on condition of anonymity, that "the committee is primarily focused on determining whether advance information about the strikes had reached the relevant agencies, which parties possessed it, and why urgent and decisive measures were not taken to address the situation before the airstrikes took place."
"The committee is carefully following the sequence of available intelligence information and the security measures that preceded the strikes to determine responsibilities and establish whether there were specific security gaps in the exchange of information and its intelligence verification and identify the parties or individuals responsible for this failure," the member added.
"Hosting the leaders and security officials will provide the committee with an opportunity to compare their statements with the information available to them," the source said, further stressing that "the hearings are part of an investigation that is not limited to determining the circumstances of the strike but also traces the information and establishes whether precautionary measures could have been taken in advance that might have prevented the casualties or reduced them."
The Iraqi government has repeatedly denied having prior knowledge of the strikes, but MPs and politicians have accused PMF leaders of possessing advance information about the targeting and failing to take sufficient precautions.
This has pushed the issue into a sensitive political arena that goes beyond the immediate security aspect.
Meanwhile, the PMF, which include the factions targeted in the strikes, rejected accusations against its chief, Falih al-Fayyadh, and claims that he had prior information about attacks on the headquarters and failed to inform the military units.
It described the accusations as "baseless claims that are not supported by any evidence or fact".
In a previous statement, the force said that "since the events in the region began months ago and until today, all its forces have been placed on alert, and two days before the strikes, all units were informed of the need to exercise the utmost caution and vigilance, which contributed to saving many lives and reducing the scale of the losses".
It said that "the fourth regiment of the 30th Brigade of the Popular Mobilisation did not take all the required preventive measures, resulting in the deaths of the largest number of its personnel during the attacks."
A sensitive issue
For his part, Iraqi political affairs specialist and academic Basim al-Azzawi said the issue was highly sensitive and that conflicting statements between accusations and denials involved political considerations.
He told TNA that "some parties may seek to use the issue of the strikes to achieve political gains, particularly given the sensitivity of the issue and its implications."
"The importance of the investigation lies in its ability to distinguish between security information and political responsibility and determine whether the failure, if established, resulted from weaknesses in the warning and information-sharing system, individual negligence by certain figures, or a broader failure in the management of the security issue," he added.
Iraqi official: PMF are part of armed forces
On Saturday, Iraqi Security Media Cell chief Lt Gen Saad Maan said that "the PMF are part of the armed forces and that the decision to restrict weapons to the state targets entities operating outside the framework of the security institutions."
Maan made the remarks to the official Iraqi News Agency, INA.
"The PMF are part of the Iraqi armed forces, and their personnel are subject to the applicable military laws," he said.
He explained that "the entities covered by the restriction of weapons are those operating outside the framework of the state's security institutions".
"The PMF are part of the Iraqi armed forces, and under Law No. 40 of 2016, all its personnel are subject to the applicable military laws," Maan added.
He said that "the decision to restrict weapons to the state is intended to affirm that there is no parallel leadership or other leadership using weapons outside the framework of the state".
Sources inside the PMF in Iraq said on Wednesday, 12 August, that major changes are expected within the force, including the replacement of its current chief, Falih al-Fayyadh, who has been at this post since being formally appointed in 2020.
The changes also include the replacement of PMF Chief of Staff Abdul Aziz al-Muhammadawi, known as Abu Fadak.
He emerged publicly and assumed his post after his predecessor, Jamal Jaafar, known as Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was assassinated by a US airstrike in January 2020.
The sources added to TNA that the changes are the first steps towards further integrating the PMF into Iraq's regular security and military system amid US pressure to restrict the weapons of Iran-aligned factions that are incorporated into and funded by the PMF itself.

articles.title: Houthis claim attack on Saudi military ship, four escort vessels in Red Sea
articles.body:
Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Monday they had attacked what they described as a Saudi military ship and four escort vessels in the Red Sea with missiles, according to a statement by the group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree on Telegram.
“The attack was carried out using several ballistic missiles, and the strikes were accurate and direct," the statement read.
"The operation resulted in the Saudi warship catching fire completely; several of the boats escorting it sank, while the others caught fire. The armed forces continue to establish the equation of blockade for blockade and to attack all Saudi military concentrations.”
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on the attack.
Houthi attacks on 'Saudi-backed forces' in Mocha
Yemen's Mocha port, near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea has suspended commercial and maritime operations after being hit by more than 25 missiles in Houthi attacks over recent days, the port's director said on Saturday.
The attacks killed seven people and caused an estimated $16 million in losses, the director told a news conference.
Forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognized government control the port. It has a smaller cargo capacity than Yemen's main ports of Aden and Hodeidah.
Yemen's government said on Friday the Houthis fired six ballistic missiles at Mocha that day, killing at least four civilians and targeting civilian, economic, and maritime facilities.
Following the attacks, the Houthis said they targeted a military build-up of weapons and warships belonging to Saudi-backed forces in Mocha.

articles.title: Ukraine Is Unleashing Flamingo Missiles on Russia at Nearly Twice the Pace of Six Months Ago
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Is Unleashing Flamingo Missiles on Russia at Nearly Twice the Pace of Six Months Ago
Ukraine is turning its homegrown Flamingo cruise missile from a rare deep-strike weapon into a recurring threat for Russia.
Ukraine has sharply increased its use of domestically produced Flamingo cruise missiles against targets inside Russia this summer, with the pace of attacks nearly doubling over the past six months, Russian media outlet Agentstvo reported on August 15.
Russian media reached the conclusion after analyzing figures released by Russia’s Defense Ministry, which point to a significant increase in reported Flamingo launches since February.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Agentstvo, Russia’s Defense Ministry has claimed to have intercepted at least 57 Flamingo missiles since June. By comparison, Moscow reported 31 interceptions between February and May.
The reported pace has accelerated further in recent weeks. Russian authorities claimed that at least 25 Flamingo missiles were shot down in just the past two weeks.
Those figures are based on Russian military statements and do not necessarily reflect the actual number of missiles launched or intercepted.
At least four Flamingo strikes have been independently confirmed this summer, including attacks against facilities linked to Russia’s military-industrial complex.
The increase suggests that Ukraine is moving the Flamingo from a weapon used in relatively limited numbers toward a more regular role in its long-range strike campaign against Russian military and industrial targets.
The missile is domestically produced, giving Ukraine greater freedom to determine how and where it is used compared with some Western-supplied weapons that have previously come with restrictions on strikes inside Russia.
If the current launch tempo continues, the Flamingo could become an increasingly important element of Ukraine’s campaign to pressure Russia’s military infrastructure far beyond the front line.
In addition, Ukrainian Fire Point FP-1 drones struck Wildberries’ largest warehouse in Russia’s Moscow region, causing a large fire at the logistics complex in Koledino.
The company said the Koledino facility covers about 250,000 square meters and is used to store, sort, and distribute dual-use goods.
Earlier, reports emerged that Ukraine sent 600 drones toward the Moscow region over 24 hours, the largest number recorded heading toward the Russian capital since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
