articles.title: Russia Is Paying Five Times More for Every Dollar Ukraine Spends on Strikes
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Is Paying Five Times More for Every Dollar Ukraine Spends on Strikes
Ukraine’s Armed Forces are inflicting losses on Russia worth several times more than the cost of the weapons used to cause them, according to data tracked by the Mission Control module of Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system, the Ministry of Defense reported on August 17.
The numbers offer a detailed look at the economics of Ukraine’s battlefield strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Mission Control data for June, every $1 Ukraine spent on engaging Russian targets produced approximately $5 in estimated losses for Russia.
Mission Control was launched six months ago and has rapidly become a major source of battlefield data for Ukrainian commanders.
The system now processes around 50,000 combat missions every week, along with more than 230,000 reports documenting their results.
Every mission is recorded, allowing Ukrainian units to examine whether an operation succeeded, identify what worked and what failed, determine why, and adjust tactics for future missions.
The system also calculates how much Ukraine spends, on average, to engage different types of targets.
In June, the average cost was approximately $3,032 per Russian servicemember targeted, $2,674 per piece of military equipment, and $1,487 per infrastructure target, according to the Defense Ministry.
For comparison, Mission Control estimates that sustaining a single Russian servicemember costs Moscow approximately $65,000.
That cost disparity is particularly important for Ukraine, which is increasingly trying to maximize the battlefield effect of relatively inexpensive drones, precision weapons, and other strike systems against higher-value Russian personnel, equipment, and infrastructure.
Mission Control does more than calculate the cost of individual strikes.
The system categorizes missions by purpose, including reconnaissance, strikes, logistics, and evacuation. It also tracks how deep units operate, including missions conducted beyond 20 kilometers and 50 kilometers from the front.
Commanders can examine which weapons and systems individual units are using, how effectively they are employing them, and how much each successful engagement costs.
The platform separately records Ukrainian equipment losses, allowing military planners to determine the conditions and distances at which vehicles, drones, and other systems are most likely to be lost.
That creates a feedback loop in which battlefield performance can be measured not only by whether a target was hit, but by how much it cost, which weapon worked best, how far from the front it was used, and what Ukraine lost in the process.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry says the growing pool of data allows units to adapt faster as battlefield conditions change and improve the efficiency of future combat missions.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia suffered nearly 43,000 battlefield casualties in July 2026, making it the Russian military’s highest monthly loss figure since January 2025, while Ukrainian forces recorded their largest territorial gains in more than a year.

articles.title: Russia jails opposition politician for 11 years for anti-war comments
articles.body:
Russia jails anti-war politician for 11 years in further clampdown on dissent
LONDON, Aug 17 - A senior member of Russia's liberal Yabloko party was sentenced on Monday to 11 years and one month in a penal colony for condemning the war in Ukraine, which he described at his trial as a catastrophe for Russia.
Lev Shlosberg, the party's deputy chairman, was accused of discrediting Russia's armed forces and spreading false information about them.
In a closing speech to the court in the city of Pskov last Friday, he maintained his innocence, said he was the victim of a political trial and repeated his call for an immediate ceasefire in the 4-1/2-year war.
The verdict, published by the court, follows an August 10 decision by Russia's Supreme Court to exclude Yabloko from taking part in a parliamentary election next month. The Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal against that ban.
Yabloko, the only registered political party to call for an end to the war, has come under heavy pressure from the authorities in the run-up to the election, where any sizeable anti-war vote could have embarrassed the Kremlin.
'LIST OF MARTYRS'
Shlosberg used his closing speech to deliver a searing indictment of the war.
"The lives of countless thousands of people have been cut short during this time. Sooner or later, the precise and complete death toll - with names included - will be made public, and the entire nation will shudder at this list of martyrs," he said, according to a transcript by independent news outlet Mediazona.
"Today, cemeteries in our country, including military ones, are growing far more rapidly than maternity wards, kindergartens, and schools," he said.
Mediazona and the BBC Russian service have recorded the names of at least 239,354 Russian military dead, based on publicly available records.
Based on records of the estates of dead people, which they used to calculate excess mortality among Russian men, they estimate the true toll at more than 350,000.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine publishes up-to-date casualty figures.
Moscow says it is fighting to address security threats from NATO and Ukraine, and to defend the rights of Russian-speakers living in Ukraine. Kyiv and its Western allies reject these as a false premise for launching the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War Two.
TRIED UNDER POST-INVASION CENSORSHIP LAWS
Russia passed laws soon after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 that prescribed long prison terms for those found guilty of "discrediting" the military or deliberately spreading false information about the war.
As a result, public condemnation of it is rarely heard inside the country. But individuals such as Shlosberg, human rights campaigner Oleg Orlov and the late dissident Alexei Navalny, defending themselves at trials with no realistic chance of acquittal, have seized the opportunity to speak out from the dock against what they have described as tyranny and repression.
Such criticism is not reported by state media, but can be read online by those with access to virtual private networks that allow them to bypass state-imposed internet restrictions and get access to websites that would otherwise be blocked.
Mediazona said Shlosberg's speech was repeatedly interrupted by the judge, who urged him to stick to the facts of the case against him. But he insisted on his right to continue.
"A single person is imprisoned, yet fear seeps into the hearts of millions," he said.
The politician was first detained in June last year and charged with discrediting the army after describing the war in Ukraine as a game of "bloody chess" in a video debate.
Prosecutors later added a charge of spreading fake news about the war in a repost on his Telegram channel.
Monday's verdict follows the conviction in June of Yabloko's deputy leader Maxim Kruglov, who was jailed for seven years for spreading lies about the army. REUTERS

articles.title: The Other Side of Paradise: How Pakistan Crushed Protests in Kashmir
articles.body:
Irish poets and American presidents have long spoken of Kashmir: its beauty and its dangers.
The question of Kashmir has shaped the trajectories of India and Pakistan since the end of British rule and their birth as nation-states in August 1947. Both countries claim Kashmir in its entirety, have fought multiple wars over it, and each controls a separate part of the territory. Historically, references to Kashmir have largely focused on the dispute between India and Pakistan, or on the most visible troubles in Indian-administered Kashmir.
Global attention has rarely lingered on the part of Kashmir administered by Pakistan. Yet, since an outbreak of protests in the region in June, more than 80 people have been killed by security forces. A different kind of political struggle has been gathering momentum there—one that is less a contest over sovereignty than an expression of long-simmering grievances over the conditions of daily life, from unaffordable electricity bills and rising food prices to a scarcity of jobs.
Pakistan-administered Kashmir has not been insulated from the wider economic crisis in Pakistan. Rising prices, fiscal pressures, energy deficits, and repeated International Monetary Fund bailouts have pushed successive governments to reduce subsidies and raise utility prices. The people of the region, already squeezed by inflation and unemployment, experience these policies not as fiscal prudence but as evidence of how little influence they have over the decisions that shape their lives.
Kashmir and the making of a protest movement
Kashmir is home to major hydropower projects that feed Pakistan’s national grid, and many residents argue that local tariffs should better reflect the territory’s contribution to power generation. The grievance is not new: protests over rising electricity and basic commodity prices have erupted periodically since 2022.
The failures of the local government to resolve these issues created an opening for a new form of political organization. Citizens committees emerged across districts, bringing together traders, lawyers, students, and community leaders. In September 2023, these committees coalesced into the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a unified body intended to coordinate mobilization across the region.
The JAAC initially demanded lower wheat and electricity prices, an end to official privileges for ministers and bureaucrats, and empowered elected local governments. It has remained outside Pakistan’s political party system. Rather than aligning with the major parties—the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz), the Pakistan People’s Party, and the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf—it presented itself as a nonpartisan platform.
The movement’s appeal seems to rest on its ability to unite constituencies across partisan divides around everyday economic and governance concerns. In response to the JAAC’s organizing, authorities arrested its members on criminal charges and restricted its meetings. But these measures failed to subdue the movement, which pressed on through shutdowns, transportation strikes, and local protests. The protest movement’s strength lies in its decentralized structure, with its chapters across small towns and villages offering a grassroots network that can be activated across the region.
In May 2024, after the government pledged to consider its demands but delayed making any substantive concessions, the JAAC called a long march and a shutdown strike. The mobilization drew hundreds of thousands of protesters toward the capital, Muzaffarabad, in one of the largest episodes of mass mobilization in the region’s history. Attempts to prevent the march backfired, broadening the movement. Protests continued to swell in Muzaffarabad despite arrests, roadblocks, and restrictions on internet and cellular communications.
Clashes during the May 2024 march left at least four people dead, including three protestors and a police officer. Islamabad ultimately intervened with a relief package reportedly worth about 23 billion rupees ($82.9 million), which included subsidized electricity tariffs and lower wheat prices. But the government’s repressive response turned a campaign over utility prices into a broader test of whether the people of Pakistan-administered Kashmir could exercise meaningful political agency.
Citizens or subjects?
The May 2024 settlement demonstrated that collective action could compel Islamabad to address immediate economic grievances. But it did not resolve the broader issue of political accountability: how Pakistan-administered Kashmir is governed? The territory has its own president, government, legislative assembly, and courts, but Pakistan retains decisive influence over key administrative, security, and external affairs.
A council chaired by Pakistan’s prime minister used to be a major source of Islamabad’s formal control over legislation, finances, and development planning. Although a constitutional amendment in 2018 stripped many of its powers, reducing it to a largely advisory body, significant authority still rests with the federal government. Key civil servants—including the chief secretary and the inspector general of police—are appointed by Islamabad, leaving the regional elected government with limited control over crucial aspects of administration.
Pakistan has long defended this exceptional arrangement in Kashmir as necessary for an exceptional situation: administering a territory whose international status remains contested. For residents, however, it has created a persistent gap between political responsibility and political authority. Elected politicians are expected to answer to voters, but the decisions that shape their daily lives are made in Islamabad.
The electoral system of the region adds another layer of complexity. The legislature of Pakistan-administered Kashmir has 53 seats. Eight of those seats are reserved for women, religious scholars, technocrats, and overseas citizens. Lawmakers are elected for the remaining 45 seats through elections. Thirty-three of those lawmakers are elected by the people living in the region. Twelve more seats in the legislature are reserved for refugees from Indian-administered Kashmir who live elsewhere in Pakistan—an arrangement introduced in the 1960s and formalized in the 1970s. Critics argue that these 12 seats significantly dilute the political weight of the territory’s voters and make it easier for whichever party rules in Islamabad to shape the assembly’s composition.
In June, the top court of the region ruled that those 12 seats enjoy statutory protection, and that any change would require a formal constitutional amendment. The ruling affirmed the government’s legal position, but it did not address the political question at the heart of the dispute. Can a legislature in which more than a quarter of directly elected seats are filled from outside the territory truly reflect the will of the people who live there?
The trouble with military hegemony
The dominant role of Pakistan’s military further constrains political space. Pakistan is governed by a hybrid regime in which civilian governments function within boundaries imposed by the military, which continues to exert tutelary control over national security, foreign policy, and even political competition. Pakistan-administered Kashmir reflects a concentrated version of this wider political order.
The geopolitical stakes of the Kashmir dispute are high, leaving the room for independent political action quite narrow. The Pakistan Army’s 12th Infantry Division, commanded by a major general and headquartered in the hill town of Murree, exercises operational control over the region, giving the military a direct hand in maintaining security.
Human rights observers have long documented the influence and the abuses of Pakistan’s military and intelligence services in the territory. The JAAC and rights activists argue that organized political activity and free expression are readily treated as security threats, narrowing the room for dissent. Elected institutions, they say, are reduced to a facade while the security apparatus determines whether political discontent can be expressed and mobilized.
The consequences of this militarized approach were on display during the renewed mobilization in the summer. In June, Pakistani authorities banned the JAAC under anti-terrorism laws, declaring it a threat to public order, and launched a broader crackdown on protesters ahead of regional assembly elections planned for Jul. 27 to Aug. 10. In late July, scores of protesters were killed, according to the leaders of the JAAC. Pakistan defended the tactics of its security forces, and a federal minister described the protesters as “militants.” While the number of civilians killed remains contested, but the political significance of the state’s response is clearer: treating a largely peaceful movement rooted in economic and democratic demands as a terrorist group reinforced the perception among the JAAC’s supporters that Islamabad would rather break heads than count them.
The JAAC had called for a boycott of the vote, making the abolition of the 12 refugee seats one of its central demands. The first phase of voting recorded a turnout of about 46%, while officials put turnout in the second phase at roughly 50%, lower than the 60% recorded in the previous two elections in 2016 and 2021. Voting in the third phase was postponed because of continued unrest.
Preliminary results gave the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz, the governing party of Pakistan, 24 general seats, though the delayed contests meant the election had yet to be finalized. The results lend credence to the JAAC’s contention that polling alone cannot resolve who exercises meaningful political authority in Kashmir. This is particularly true when the ruling party in Islamabad can draw on state resources and the military establishment’s backing to shape both the electoral environment and, ultimately, the composition of the legislature.
This manipulation begins well before polling day. Critics say officers from Pakistan’s Inter-Services Intelligence and Military Intelligence, operating under the area’s army command structure, use pressure tactics and patronage to favor candidates who endorse Kashmir’s integration with Pakistan. The 12 refugee seats, critics argue, are not simply a constitutional problem but an additional lever through which politically loyal candidates can be brought into the assembly.
The movement’s durability suggests that it is more than a dispute over economic disparities; it reflects a broader crisis of affordability, legitimacy, and accountability. In that sense, the deeper shift is one of political expectations. Support for the JAAC, particularly among young people, reflects a growing impatience with political subordination justified as a geopolitical imperative.
The unrest also reveals an uncomfortable contradiction in Pakistan’s official position on Kashmir. For decades, Islamabad has accused India, not without justification, of gross human rights violations against Kashmiris on its side of the Line of Control. Pakistan’s foreign policy rests on the claim that Kashmiris possess a moral and legal “right of self-determination” and that Kashmir’s final status should be decided through a United Nations-administered plebiscite. Yet those claims are difficult to sustain when Islamabad’s own governance of Pakistan-administered Kashmir falls short of the very standards it invokes in criticizing India.
For Islamabad, the lesson is clear. Stability cannot be bought with temporary economic relief that leaves the underlying structure of political power intact. Nor can it be secured through repression, which amplifies alienation, fuels anger, and breeds broader resentment toward the Pakistani state. Stability depends on meaningfully addressing the local demand for responsive and credible government, and on recognizing that the people of Pakistan-administered Kashmir are citizens with political rights, not supplicants dependent on Islamabad’s largesse.
Kashmiris are not merely demanding lower bills and cheaper bread. They are demanding respect and representation. In the towns and valleys of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, these aspirations cannot simply be suppressed by force.

articles.title: Poland has not yet made a decision on Patriot missiles for Ukraine, but the US is pressing - government official
articles.body:
Poland has not yet made a decision on Patriot missiles for Ukraine, but the US is pressing - government official
Kyiv • UNN
Polish Deputy Defence Minister Cezary Tomczyk said that a decision on transferring Patriot missiles to Ukraine has not yet been made. He noted that the US, in particular General Hrynkevych, is actively urging the Polish government to do so.
Poland has not yet made a decision on providing Ukraine with additional Patriot missiles, but the Americans are pressuring the Polish government over these interceptors, Poland's Deputy Minister of National Defence Cezary Tomczyk said on air on Polskie Radio 24, UNN reports.
Details
Tomczyk was asked whether Poland would provide Ukraine with Patriot missiles. "No decisions have been made on this matter," Tomczyk said. He recalled that Poland has so far supported Ukraine with several such missiles "out of the hundreds we have." He assured that Poland is safe. "Polish stocks are full, secure, and being replenished," he added.
He noted that any decision to transfer missiles must be made at the highest level. "First, the Minister of National Defence submits recommendations, and then the Council of Ministers makes the decision," he explained the procedure.
"Ukraine's main need today is protection against ballistic missiles. Cities such as Kyiv and Lviv are attacked by Russia every day. Obviously, Ukraine is asking its Western partners to provide or enable the purchase of missiles for Patriot systems," the Polish deputy defence minister said.
He stressed that Poland receives most of the calls from the United States.
"It is precisely the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Grynkiewicz, as well as the US administration, who very often convey these appeals to the Polish government to provide missiles for Patriot systems whenever possible," he acknowledged.

articles.title: ‘Voluntary donations’ by Russian businesses to state budget hit a record sum since start of 2026
articles.body:
‘Voluntary donations’ by Russian businesses to state budget hit a record sum since start of 2026
Russian businesses made 383.69 billion rubles in non-repayable contributions to the federal budget during the first eight months of 2026 — almost one and a half times the total for all of last year.
The Russian business daily Vedomosti reported the figures after reviewing data from the government’s Electronic Budget information system, calling them the highest contributions recorded since this line item was added to the Tax Code.
In previous years, most of the money under this line item — which appeared in the Tax Code only in 2022 — came from the “exit tax” paid by departing foreign businesses. In 2026, though, the biggest source became “voluntary donations” from major Russian businessmen.
The idea of “voluntary donations” first surfaced in March, during a private meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and the country’s leading businessmen. The Kremlin insisted the idea had come from the businessmen themselves, but sources, including the independent Russian media outlet The Bell, reported that Putin himself had proposed the businessmen fund the war in Ukraine.
Vedomosti, citing data published on the Finance Ministry’s website, wrote that most of the money came in after March: “voluntary donations” to the federal budget totaled 15.6 billion rubles from January through March, then jumped tenfold in April to 159.7 billion rubles, and rose another 45.5% in May to 232.3 billion rubles.
Russia’s budget deficit, driven by the ongoing war in Ukraine, reached 6.455 trillion rubles — 2.8% of GDP — between January and July 2026, exceeding the government’s planned targets.

Russia's anti-war Yabloko party loses appeal against removal from elections
Russia's Supreme Court has upheld a decision to remove the anti-war Yabloko party from the elections to the State Duma the lower house of the Russian parliament , while at least 60 people were detained outside the court.
Source: BBC News Russian; Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's Russian Service
Details: The ruling was issued on 17 August.
The court rejected all motions by Yabloko's lawyers to admit additional materials and dismissed the party's appeal.
Representatives of the Prosecutor General's Office and the Central Election Commission had called for the party to be removed from the election. The commission had registered Yabloko's candidate list less than three weeks earlier.
Reports in the media said at least 60 people had been detained outside the court.
Members of Yabloko – Russia's only party to oppose the war against Ukraine – support a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace, and oppose nuclear war and political repression.

- It is the first time in modern Russian history that a party that was registered to take part in an election has been removed from the ballot.
- On 11 August, a Russian court sentenced Lev Shlosberg, deputy leader of the anti-war Yabloko party, to 11 years and one month in prison after finding him guilty of "discrediting the armed forces" and spreading "fake war news".

articles.title: Trump says Iran should surrender, threatens to bomb Oman
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump says Iran should surrender, threatens to bomb Oman
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that Iran should surrender to end a war with the US as talks between the countries remained stalled.
"They should put up the white flag of surrender," Trump told a Fox News reporter during a phone interview.
An interim deal agreed to in June declared an "immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts", but quickly unraveled, with Trump saying it was "over" on July 7 and Iran's foreign ministry declaring it "suspended" a week later.
Under that memorandum of understanding, Iran and the U.S. committed to negotiating a final deal — covering broader issues such as the fate of Iran's nuclear programme — in a maximum of 60 days, extendable by mutual consent. Monday marks 60 days since the MOU was signed.
Separately, Oman and Iran have been in talks to try to reach an agreement to restore commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which carried 20% of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before the U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran began in late February.
"If Oman gets in the way, we'll bomb the shit out of them," Trump told Fox.
The dispute over control of the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel prices and put pressure on Trump to end a war that is unpopular at home ahead of the November midterm elections that will decide control of the US Congress.
Trump told Fox News that the midterms were not impacting his strategy on Iran.
"Midterms have nothing to do with my thinking," he said.
Earlier on Monday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform: "The number one Goal is, and always will be, that Iran cannot have, in any way, shape, or form, a Nuclear Weapon," repeating one of his stated rationales for the war.

articles.title: Iranian drones attack Iraqi Kurdistan PM Barzani's office
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iranian drones attack Iraqi Kurdistan PM Masrour Barzani's office
Two Iranian drones targeted the Iraqi Kurdistan prime minister's office and the home of the autonomous region's intelligence chief overnight, authorities said Monday.
"Following an investigation by the Kurdistan Counter-Terrorism Unit, my personal office and the home of the head of the Security and Intelligence Agency were targeted by Iranian drone attacks earlier today," Kurdistan Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said, in a post on X.
"This is a dangerous escalation and a direct threat to the security and stability of the Kurdistan region," the posted added.
The regional Counter-Terrorism Directorate said there were no casualties in the attack.
"Two Hadid-110 type explosive-laden drones were launched from across the Iranian border toward the private office of the Kurdistan region prime minister and the residence of the Parastin Agency director," it said.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, the Iraqi Kurdistan region, which hosts US troops and foreign oil firms as well as rebels exiled from Iran, has been targeted with more than 1,000 attacks by Tehran and pro-Iran armed groups inside Iraq.
Drones have repeatedly been intercepted over Kurdistan's capital Erbil, while others have struck the rebels and US interests.
Tehran accuses the exiled Kurdish opposition groups of serving Western and Israeli interests, and continued to launch strikes against them even during a regional ceasefire announced in April, which eventually broke down.
The groups have mostly evacuated their bases and camps in Kurdistan since the war began.
On 17 July, drone and rocket strikes killed nine people near the Iraqi city of Sulaimaniyah in the region's east.

articles.title: South Korea hopes for U.S.–North Korea talks after military drills are scaled back
articles.body:
South Korea hopes for U.S.–North Korea talks after military drills are scaled back
Kyiv • UNN
Seoul is counting on the resumption of talks between Washington and Pyongyang following Trump's order to scale back joint military exercises. Experts doubt Kim Jong Un will quickly agree because of his nuclear capabilities and cooperation with Russia.
South Korea expressed hope for the resumption of meaningful dialogue between the United States and North Korea after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a significant reduction in joint military exercises. AP reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
On Monday, South Korea and the United States began the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield summer exercises. At the same time, Seoul is concerned that the reduction in the exercises could affect the allies’ readiness to respond to threats from North Korea
Trump said he had instructed U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth to "substantially reduce" the scale of the exercises. The American president explained this by citing their high cost and the fact that they allegedly send North Korea an "absolutely inappropriate and hostile signal."
Seoul wants dialogue to resume
The South Korean presidential administration said it hoped to use the good relations between Trump and Kim Jong Un to initiate meaningful dialogue between Washington and Pyongyang.
Seoul said it was ready to make the necessary diplomatic efforts to discuss peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung had also previously advocated improving relations with North Korea.
At the same time, experts doubt that Kim Jong Un will quickly agree to return to negotiations. In their view, the North Korean leader may demand significant concessions from the United States, given the development of North Korea’s nuclear capabilities and its military cooperation with Russia.

articles.title: European Solidarity proposes moratorium on business inspections, war risk insurance
articles.body:
The European Solidarity party proposes introducing an economic resilience package to support Ukrainian business during a difficult period, which would include war risk insurance, accessible financing for recovery after Russian attacks, a moratorium on law enforcement pressure and inspections, protection of logistics hubs and critical warehouses, export support programs, and predictable rules for entrepreneurs, reported party leader and Member of Parliament of Ukraine Petro Poroshenko.
"Exports have been halted, which significantly deepens the crisis. Part of Ukrainian business today is definitely not talking about development. People are talking about how to simply survive and avoid bankruptcy. Following Russian strikes on warehouses and trade infrastructure in certain cities, supply disruptions are unfortunately occurring. And this is certainly no longer just an economic issue. Because a food warehouse today is just as much an element of the state's resilience as a power plant... During war, business does not need inspectors or additional tax audits from the state. It needs protection: war risk insurance, access to financing, state protection of critical logistics, a moratorium on pointless inspections and pressure from law enforcement, export support, and mechanisms for the rapid recovery of enterprises after Russian attacks," Poroshenko said in a video address on Monday.
According to him, "this is precisely what a wartime economy is—not an economy where the state commands business, but an economy where the state takes its hands off the throats of those who fill the budget and fund the army."
The leader of European Solidarity also reported that the economic resilience plan is part of an action plan that will be submitted to the Verkhovna Rada. The plan also encompasses programs for protecting citizens' lives, budgetary priority for funding the army and defense, development of military technology, a roadmap for the country's energy resilience, European integration, and establishing government accountability.
"European Solidarity is ready to support every decision that gives more weapons to the army, more opportunities to Ukrainian producers, more protection to business, more independence to the judiciary, and leads Ukraine faster to the European Union. We will certainly not vote for corruption, new barriers for entrepreneurs, official arbitrariness, or yet another budget attraction of populism. A country fighting for survival cannot afford an inefficient state," Poroshenko said.

Russia Recruited Nearly 3,000 Africans From 37 Countries For Its War Against Ukraine
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry says at least 2,982 people from 37 African countries have been recruited into Russia’s armed forces, with around 486 killed in the war against Ukraine.
The figures were provided by the ministry in response to a request from Suspilne on August 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Foreign Ministry, 35 citizens of 17 African countries are currently being held as prisoners of war in Ukraine. The largest numbers of recruits have reportedly come from Kenya, Egypt, Cameroon, Ghana, Nigeria, Uganda, Algeria, and Mali.
“To recruit Africans, Russian intelligence services employ a wide range of manipulative methods aimed at coercion and deception, including under the pretext of offering civilian employment or education, promising high financial compensation, prospects of obtaining Russian citizenship, or other migration and social benefits,” the ministry said.
In some cases, foreign nationals are pressured into signing military contracts written in Russian under the threat of deportation or imprisonment.
Ukraine is seeking to counter the recruitment campaign through its diplomatic missions in Africa. Ukrainian diplomats regularly inform local officials about cases of Russian recruitment of their citizens and conduct public information campaigns in countries where Ukraine maintains diplomatic representation.
The Foreign Ministry, together with Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, has also launched a dedicated website available in English, French, and Swahili.
According to Suspine, the resource provides verified information about Russian recruitment methods, accounts from people affected by the campaign, analytical materials, practical guidance for potential victims and their families, and channels for reporting suspected recruiters, according to the ministry.
Similar cases have also been reported in other countries. The Peruvian government, for example, has confirmed that 11 of its citizens who joined Russian forces have been killed, while 114 remain missing and three have been captured by Ukrainian forces.
According to Spanish news agency EFE, Peruvian authorities said that among Peruvians recruited into the Russian military were people who are now missing or being held captive by Ukraine.
Overall, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate has identified more than 28,000 foreign nationals serving in the Russian Armed Forces under military contracts, with the number continuing to rise.

EU Prepares Largest Sanctions Package Yet Aimed at Crippling Russian War Effort
The European Union is preparing its largest sanctions effort to date against Moscow to expand its current blacklist by one-third.
European Union top diplomat Kaja Kallas stated that European restrictions have already cost Russia over €1 trillion ($1.08 trillion), while the previous 21st package enacted on July 23 designated 170 entities and 48 individuals—including major banks, cryptocurrency networks, oil traders, energy sector assets, and shadow fleet vessels—bringing total listings close to 3,000, as reported by Die Welt.

"If it is adopted, the number of sanctioned Russian individuals, companies, and organizations will immediately increase by a third. Pressure must be increased until Russia stops the war," Kallas stated.
Although details of the new restrictions remain undisclosed, Kallas noted that the introduction of a Russian sanctions bill in the US Senate, initiated by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, "gives hope for alignment between Europe and the United States."
Insiders cited by Bloomberg in late July indicated that the European Union intends to target more than 1,600 additional companies connected to Russia. These businesses generate over $20 billion in combined annual revenue and employ 265,000 workers.
The prospective restrictions are set to target previously unlisted enterprises within the Russian defense-industrial complex. However, reports suggest the financial strain of this upcoming round will prove less severe than earlier measures against banking institutions and oil exports.
European Union foreign ministers are scheduled to review and potentially approve the package during their meeting in October.
Previously, Kallas announced that EU naval forces operating in the Mediterranean have been granted the authority to board vessels suspected of being part of Russia’s shadow fleet.

articles.title: Jordan's king courts China while keeping Washington close
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Jordan's King Abdullah courts China while keeping Washington close
Jordan’s King Abdullah II departed for China on Monday seeking deeper economic ties with Beijing at a moment when his country is trying to navigate an increasingly complicated relationship with the world’s major powers.
The trip is not a pivot away from Washington, Jordan’s most important security partner and a major source of aid. But, Jordanian officials and analysts see it as part of a broader effort by Amman to widen its options, particularly on investment, technology and infrastructure, while preserving an alliance with the United States that remains central to the kingdom’s security.
King Abdullah is expected to meet on Tuesday with President Xi Jinping, Premier Li Qiang and Zhao Leji, chairman of the Standing Committee of China’s National People’s Congress, according to Jordan’s Royal Court. He is also travelling with an economic delegation and is due to meet executives from major Chinese companies.
The visit comes as Jordan faces mounting pressures from conflicts around it and seeks a larger role in regional diplomacy. Amman has maintained contacts with both Washington and Tehran in recent months while trying to shield itself from the fallout of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Nidal al-Taani, former chairman of the Jordanian parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, said the kingdom had long sought to diversify its political and economic partnerships.
The China trip, he said, amounted to a “policy of diversifying partnerships, not a policy of disengagement”.
That distinction is important for Jordan.
The United States remains deeply embedded in the kingdom’s security and defence architecture, while Jordan’s geography gives it an importance to Washington that far exceeds the relatively modest size of its economy.
But Amman also sees an opportunity in China, particularly as Beijing expands its economic and diplomatic presence across the region.
Taani described Jordan as an “important gateway and transit point” for future regional arrangements, arguing that its location and relationships with competing powers give it an important diplomatic role.
For Jordan, the challenge is to turn closer ties with China into tangible economic gains without provoking retribution by Washington.
Hassan Abdullah Al-Dajeh, a member of the World Council for Chinese Studies, said Beijing could offer Jordan investment, technology, infrastructure financing and greater access to Chinese markets.
The king’s decision to bring an economic delegation and meet Chinese business leaders, he said, underscored the commercial ambitions behind the trip.
But there are limits to how far that relationship can go.
Chinese investment in energy, water, transport and civilian technology would be relatively straightforward, Dajeh said. Greater Chinese involvement in sensitive telecommunications networks, dual-use ports, security-related artificial intelligence or defence procurement could prove far more difficult because of Jordan’s extensive military and intelligence cooperation with the United States.
“Amman can look east economically, but the ceiling of its manoeuvring remains governed by its security alliance with the United States and its ability to reassure both sides,” Dajeh said.
Jordan has little incentive to choose between the two powers.
Instead, its approach reflects a strategy increasingly visible among regional governments that retain close security relationships with Washington while looking to China for investment, trade and technology.

articles.title: Kushner sits with Netanyahu to talk Gaza after 2-hour meeting with Hamas
articles.body:
Marathon US-Israel meeting produces optimism but no firm commitment to American plan for Gaza
JERUSALEM (AP) — A marathon meeting Monday between U.S. negotiator Jared Kushner and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu left the fate of the Gaza ceasefire unclear, with officials signaling moderate optimism but offering no concrete commitment by Israel to the latest U.S.-proposed plan.
Hamas has already agreed to the proposal. American negotiators appeared to acquiesce to Israeli demands that Hamas disarmament must come before any reconstruction of the devastated Palestinian enclave. They did not publicly signal that Israel had made any commitments to withdraw from the 60% of Gaza that Israeli troops currently occupy.
That’s a major sticking point in the plan and one that Hamas had pressed negotiators to compel Israel to fulfill prior to the meeting. The talks came days after Netanyahu rejected the 15-point, U.S.-backed road map to move the ceasefire deal forward, saying there would be no withdrawal without disarmament.
A day earlier, Kushner met for two hours with Hamas’ leader in Egypt.
Former British Prime Minister Tony Blair and the director of the U.S.-created Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, were also in the meeting with Netanyahu, according to a source familiar with the plans and a diplomatic source. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
At stake are the lives of some 2 million Palestinians in Gaza, rebuilding plans and future control over the territory.
Netanyahu says talks were ‘deep and constructive’
In a statement, Netanyahu’s office said the talks were “deep and constructive.” Israel and the board agreed to establish two working groups — one on the disarmament and demilitarization of Gaza and another focused on public health issues for Gaza.
Israel and the board agreed that the demilitarization “should be prompt and completed before any reconstruction,” the statement said.
A Board of Peace official said they also agreed that the demilitarization must include “every weapon, light and heavy, and every tunnel.” The official spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meeting.
“Backed by President Donald Trump, the parties share clear goals: a fully demilitarized and deradicalized Gaza that poses no threat to Israel, and where Gazans can pursue prosperity and dignity peacefully,” the official said.
Another Board of Peace official said the meeting was “very productive” and resulted in agreement on “a path forward.”
“The Israelis are going to give this a chance. Now it’s up to Hamas to show if it truly intends to comply,” said the official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity.
Asked if Israel had committed to the U.S. plan for Gaza, a spokesperson for Mladenov said it was a “work in progress.”
Meeting followed Kushner’s conversation with Hamas
Kushner, who is Trump’s son-in-law, met Sunday with Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya in Cairo on disarmament, according to a regional official and a Hamas official, who both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to reporters.
Officials from mediating countries Egypt, Qatar and Turkey also were there.
The Hamas official said the Hamas leader demanded that Israel halt its attacks on Gaza and withdraw to the so-called “yellow line” dividing the territory before beginning implementation.
The yellow line was never precisely defined. Israeli forces have moved beyond it and now control about 60% of Gaza. In May, Netanyahu said the next step was to move to 70% control, with Israel “tightening the grip” on Hamas “from every direction.”
Several regional powers including Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates issued a statement Sunday condemning Israel’s rejection of the road map. They said Israel “now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza.” Other signers included Jordan, Pakistan, Indonesia and the ceasefire mediators.
The foreign ministers’ statement called on the Board of Peace and the U.S. to take “immediate and concrete measures” to keep any party from obstructing the plan’s implementation.
Talks spark hope and doubt in Gaza
While some in Gaza hope that efforts to implement the road map will bring an end to the war sparked by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, others are skeptical.
Mohammad Abu al-Qombuz cast doubt on all talks and visits currently taking place.
“A conference here and there, it is all lies. We need a definitive solution that would work for everybody,” said Abu al-Qombuz, who lives in a Gaza City tent camp, part of the territory’s vast displaced population.
Under the road map, Hamas would hand over weapons to the Palestinian technocratic committee meant to oversee daily operations in the territory. The committee has not yet entered Gaza.
But Hamas has linked the surrender of its heaviest weapons to the creation of a Palestinian state, and the road map entails the creation of a “credible pathway toward achieving Palestinian self-determination and statehood,” something Israel’s current government rejects.
Until the road map is agreed to, other elements of the ceasefire are on hold, including reconstruction and the deployment of international forces to separate Israeli forces from committee-controlled areas.
Netanyahu faces a challenging election on Oct. 27 as he tries to hold onto power with a coalition that includes ministers taking a harsh line on Gaza, and it’s not clear whether he will take decisive steps on the ceasefire before then.
Also coming up is the anniversary of the 2023 attack.
___
Frankel reported from Jerusalem, Magdy from Cairo and Shurafa from Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip. Associated Press journalists Sam Mednick in Tel Aviv, Israel; Collin Binkley in Washington; and Sylvia Hui in London contributed to this report.

articles.title: New Space Force EW Unit Pairs Multiple Weapon Systems in a First
articles.body:
The Space Force activated the 1st Electromagnetic Warfare Squadron earlier this month, a new unit with a few unique characteristics—it is manned mostly by former Air National Guardsmen, and it is the service’s first EW unit to be equipped with two different weapons.
Combat Forces Command said in an Aug. 14 release that the squadron activated Aug. 3 at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo. The squadron falls under Mission Delta 3.
The squadron, which will actually have personnel distributed across five locations, will operate both the new Meadowlands system and the Bounty Hunter weapon. Meadowlands is a mobile, ground-based space electronic warfare system made by L3Harris Technologies that can temporarily detect, identify, deny, disrupt and degrade adversary satellite communications and radars. Bounty Hunter is a kind of listening post and defensive EW system used to detect, characterize, geolocate, and report electromagnetic interference and signal jamming that aims to strike U.S. and allied satellite communications.
Combat Forces Command announced operational acceptance of Meadowlands in June, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported, meaning it can be used in combat missions. Meadowlands is actually a “critical upgrade” to the Counter Communications System, as it is both mobile and smaller, Space Force officials said at the time.
Bounty Hunter has been around in some form since the early 2010s and was put into operations in U.S. Pacific Command in 2018 and U.S. Central Command in 2019, hitting initial operational capability in 2020. It has gone through upgrades of its own, officials said last year.
“Combining these functions and systems within single squadrons creates a cohesive combat power and can enable better execution of both missions,” said Charles Galbreath, a retired Space Force colonel and director of space studies at the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence.
The squadron is one piece of a larger EW puzzle that’s critical to space operations.
“Since the command and control of satellites and all information from those satellites travels the electromagnetic spectrum, maintaining spectrum superiority is critical to the Space Force and the preservation of space superiority,” Galbreath told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
In June, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported that USSF wants five new Space Electromagnetic Warfare Tactical Operations Centers. Space Force officials announced last September at AFA’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference that Mission Delta 3, which includes the 1st Electromagnetic Warfare Squadron, had opened the first SEWTOC in Colorado Springs, Colo.
USSF officials did not immediately respond to an Air & Space Forces Magazine query on August 17.
Seasoned Personnel
While the squadron is new, its Guardians are not.
“Our competitive edge is the pairing decades of seasoned EW mastery with the innovation of our newest Guardians,” Lt. Col. Danielle Ryan, squadron commander, said in the release. “We are fusing deep expertise with fresh tactics, advancing our spectrum dominance.”
Of the nine space-focused Air National Guard units whose missions were transferred into the Space Force this past October, five were electromagnetic warfare squadrons, from Hawaii to Alaska. The Space Force has selected 99 Guardsman from all nine squadrons to transfer to the service in full-time roles, and still others may follow in part-time positions.
“The utilization of former [Air Force] Guardsman into the 1st [Electromagnetic Warfare Squadron] speaks to the talent and expertise that resided in the Guard and Reserve,” Galbreath said. “Through the Space Force Personnel Management Acts, these highly training experts can continue to provide effects within their specialty, but in a new status.”
The act, passed with the fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act, created one military personnel management system that lets Guardians move between full-time and part-time status without the cumbersome, legacy methods that often stalled such moves for members of other services in the past.

articles.title: 'Islamic Republic of Britain': Netanyahu compares Churchill-era support for Israel to today’s UK
articles.body:
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused Britain of abandoning its past support for Israel, branding the country the “Islamic Republic of Britain” during an interview on the Army Radio podcast King of Creating Life published last week.
On the podcast, the prime minister argued that the support Randolph Churchill and his son, Winston, showed for Israel's victory in the Six-Day War can't be found today in the "Islamic Republic of Britain.
"Incidentally, he [younger Winston Churchill] and his father, Randolph, Churchill’s son, came here and covered the Six-Day War in a way that was very favorable toward us,” Netanyahu said. “Try finding that in Britain today, in what is called the Islamic Republic of Britain.”
Netanyahu also recalled a phrase someone had said that "the first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons will be the Islamic Republic of Britain."
"We’re making sure there won’t be another one, you know, in Iran," he stated. Notably, the Islamic Republic of Pakistan has had an active nuclear program since 1972.
Khamenei posters, Iran regime flags displayed at London march
Tensions between Israel and the Britain have grown strained over the past few months, and even more so since British Prime Minister Andy Burnham took over from Keir Starmer.
Last week, open displays of support for the Islamic Regime in Iran were seen throughout Sunday’s Arbaeen Procession in London.
The Arbaeen Procession is an annual public march held to commemorate Imam Hussain ibn Ali, the grandson of Prophet Muhammad, who was martyred in Karbala, Iraq, in 680 CE.
The Jerusalem Post reviewed hundreds of videos and photos from the event, finding at least dozens of posters and flags of former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, as well as hundreds of Islamic regime flags.
One in particular stood out: a poster by the Islamic Human Rights Commission with the words “Choose the right side of history” superimposed on a photo of Khamenei.
The IHRC has been investigated by the UK’s Charity Commission since 2017 for its alleged ties to the Iranian regime.
Also visible in the footage from Sunday was a man wearing a keffiyeh featuring the three supreme leaders of the Islamic regime: erstwhile supreme leader Ruhollah Khomeini, Ali Khamenei, and Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.
The brazen displays of pro-regime propaganda during Sunday’s Arbaeen march were particularly striking given the UK’s recent introduction of the National Security (State Threats) Act 2026.
Mathilda Heller contributed to this report.

articles.title: Asia shares decline as worries about rising oil prices outweigh perks from strong earnings
articles.body:
Asian shares slip as worries about rising oil prices offset boost from strong earnings
TOKYO (AP) — Asian shares were mostly lower on Tuesday, as rising oil prices and worries about inflation countered the boost to sentiment from robust corporate earnings reports.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 sank 2.5% to 67,460.73.
South Korea’s Kospi lost 1.6% to 6,869.83. The index has been sliding recently as investors have sold shares in the local market and invested in U.S. stocks to escape wild swings in the Kospi linked to the boom in artificial intelligence, analysts said.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 was little changed, inching down less than 0.1% to 9,070.00.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.2% to 25,513.65, while the Shanghai Composite added 0.2% to 3,990.30.
Analysts said robust earnings reports in Asia and the U.S., partly tied to AI, have helped to counter worries about what the war in Iran will do to the global flow of crude oil and its impact on energy prices. Japan, for one, imports almost all its oil.
“First, the beneficiary base from AI investment has broadened. Demand spread across a wide range of industries, including semiconductor production equipment, power equipment, machinery, electronic components, and materials. AI demand effectively helped rediscover globally competitive companies across these sectors,” Masashi Akutsu and Tetsuhiro Tokuyama said in a recent report for BofA Securities.
Oil prices have crept higher after a brief respite last month driven by hopes for an end to the war with Iran.
The 60-day deadline for an agreement to end the Iran war and resolve the dispute over its nuclear program is expiring. An interim agreement reached in June has collapsed, and Washington and Tehran are even further apart than they were then.
Last month alone, Brent crude, the international standard, zigzagged between $72 and $102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again.
Early Tuesday, the price for a barrel of Brent crude rose 0.5% to $91.35 a barrel. It gained 2.7% on Monday.
Benchmark U.S. crude rose 0.8% to $85.16 a barrel.
Higher oil prices have been a major factor behind stubbornly high inflation.
On Wall Street, stocks edged further away from their record heights Monday. The S&P 500 fell 0.5% but remains near its all-time high set Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 272 points, or 0.5%, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.3%.
In currency trading early Tuesday, the U.S. dollar rose to 159.76 Japanese yen from 159.46 yen. The euro cost $1.1570, down from $1.1583.

articles.body:
Russian strikes kill 10 in Kharkiv as Ukrainian drones hit Moscow
Russian attacks reportedly killed 10 people and injured eight in Ukraine’s Kharkiv.
Ukraine launched more than 620 drones at Moscow overnight in what appeared to be its largest such attack in years, while Russian attacks killed 10 people in Ukraine’s Kharkiv region, according to Russian and Ukrainian officials.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 180 of the 620 drones heading towards Moscow were “destroyed” by Russian defences over the capital region between Monday evening and 5am (02:00 GMT) on Tuesday. He said 17 more drones were shot down en route to the capital later.

Russia’s state-run news agency TASS described the barrage as the largest drone attack on Moscow in the past two years.
The drone attack wounded three people, including a 10-year-old girl, Moscow region’s Governor Andrey Vorobyov said on Telegram. He said the “most serious consequences” were reported in the Pavlovsky Posad district, where a house burned down. Several more homes and a guesthouse were damaged in Bogorodsky district, he added.
A warehouse east of Moscow belonging to e-commerce giant Wildberries was damaged in Tuesday’s drone assault. In a statement, the company said its logistics complex sustained “minor damage” after “debris hit the wall of the building”.
Ukraine has struck multiple Wildberries warehouses in recent weeks, saying the company supplies components for Russian drones.
Ten killed in Kharkiv
Meanwhile, the Ukrainian air force reported shooting down or suppressing 111 of 147 “enemy” drones overnight.
Kharkiv’s regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said preliminary information indicated 10 people were killed and eight injured in the Pechenihy settlement.
Five others, including a nine-year-old boy, were injured in the city of Izyum, he added.
Elsewhere, Russian drones sparked fires and damaged buildings in Kyiv region’s Brovary city, including an office building and warehouses, said Mayor Ihor Sapozhko.
With front-line fighting at a near standstill and talks frozen, Ukraine and Russia have significantly stepped up long-distance attacks, pushing the civilian death toll to its highest levels since the war’s first months in 2022.
In July alone, 437 civilians were killed in Ukraine, the highest monthly toll since May 2022, according to a United Nations tally.
Russian authorities reported 79 civilians killed in Ukrainian attacks in July, up from the previous month.

“Intentional Negligence”: Russian Nuclear Power Company Accused of Safety Violations
Russia's state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom is facing allegations of safety breaches, security violations, and engineering failures at its El-Dabaa nuclear power plant project in Egypt, according to confidential documents obtained by Politico on August 17.
The Egyptian plant uses the exact same technology as the Paks II project that Rosatom is building in Hungary.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A confidential letter sent on June 4 to Rosatom's chief by the Nuclear Power Plants Authority of Egypt details physical defects across multiple reactor units and a breakdown in nuclear safety culture during construction.
The letter also highlights intentional negligence by a project official. Internal audit documents from 2025 indicate that the original construction schedule for the first reactor unit could be delayed by 18 months, shifting completion from September 2028 to March 2030.
The leaked materials were provided by an intelligence official speaking on condition of anonymity.
According to the documents, recurring defects in concrete have appeared at the site, including voids behind the metal liner on Unit 4, foundation slab issues on Units 1, 2, and 3 that required a year to repair, and structural wall defects on Unit 4.
The Egyptian authority accused Rosatom of deceptive practices and performing fake work to claim the plant was over half finished, despite visual inspections showing main reactor buildings remained underground.
The authority also cited workers consuming alcohol on site, using fake passes, and illegally sharing photos and videos of the site on social media.
In one instance, a worker who suffered a severe compound fracture was quietly moved in a private vehicle rather than an ambulance to conceal the incident.
Rosatom denied the claims, stating that it maintains the highest levels of nuclear safety throughout construction. The company noted that none of the allegations were verified through official contractual, technical, or supervisory procedures.
Rosatom declined to confirm whether it received the letter from Egyptian authorities, while the Egyptian authority did not respond to requests for comment.
Previously, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar cast doubt on a landmark agreement with Russia’s state nuclear company Rosatom to expand Hungary’s nuclear power capacity.
The announcement came after weeks of extreme heat and drought pushed the Danube River to record low levels, severely impacting power generation and cutting output at Hungary’s existing Paks nuclear plant to little more than 10%.
Although Rosatom CEO Alexei Likhachev insisted that construction of two new reactors remained on schedule, Magyar pushed back, noting that the site consisted of little more than storage depots and two concrete pits despite billions spent, prompting his administration to initiate a comprehensive review of the $11.5 billion project's financing and cooling mechanisms.
